subtopic_detail: adolescent with monthly lower abdominal pain who has never had a period and a bulging bluish membrane
stem:
You are the registrar in a paediatric emergency department seeing a 14-year-old girl brought in by her mother with lower abdominal pain. The pain has come in episodes lasting three or four days roughly every month for the past six months and is worsening; this time she has also found it difficult to pass urine and has not opened her bowels for two days.

She has never had a period. Her mother reports that she developed breasts around the age of eleven and that her growth spurt is finished. On examination she is afebrile and comfortable at rest. Breast development and pubic hair are both Tanner stage 5. There is a smooth, non-tender midline suprapubic mass that reaches halfway to the umbilicus. Inspection of the vulva shows normal external genitalia with a tense bluish membrane bulging at the introitus, which becomes more prominent when she coughs. A bladder scan shows a residual volume of 480 mL.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 88 beats per minute, blood pressure 112/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees
data_table.Examination: Tanner stage 5 breast and pubic hair development, smooth non-tender midline suprapubic mass
data_table.Vulval inspection: Normal external genitalia with a tense bluish membrane bulging at the introitus, more prominent on coughing
data_table.Investigations: Post-void bladder residual volume 480 mL on bedside scan, urinary pregnancy test negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Commence a continuous combined oral contraceptive pill to suppress her cyclical symptoms
Request a karyotype with serum testosterone and refer to the adolescent gynaecology clinic
Aspirate the collection through the membrane in the department with a wide bore needle
Insert a urinary catheter and refer for surgical incision of the obstructing membrane
Arrange an outpatient pelvic ultrasound and gynaecology clinic review within four weeks

subtopic_detail: student with cramping on the first two days of each period since her cycles became regular
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 16-year-old girl who has cramping lower abdominal pain on the first two days of every period. It began about eighteen months after her first period, which was at twelve, and has been present with every cycle since. She describes it as coming in waves low down in the middle, sometimes with an ache into her thighs and some loose bowel motions on the first day.

She has missed three days of school this term. Her cycles are regular at 29 days with four days of bleeding that soaks four pads a day, and there is no bleeding between periods. She is not sexually active. She has been taking paracetamol 1 g as needed on the worst day with partial benefit, starting once the pain is established. Abdominal examination is soft with no masses or tenderness today, and she is systemically well with no weight loss and no urinary or bowel symptoms between periods.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Soft non-tender abdomen, no palpable mass, normal secondary sexual characteristics
data_table.Menstrual history: Menarche at twelve, regular 29 day cycles, four days of bleeding, four pads per day, no intermenstrual bleeding
data_table.Current treatment: Paracetamol 1 g as required, started after pain onset, with partial benefit

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first line treatment?

options.text: Refer for a diagnostic laparoscopy to look for peritoneal deposits and adhesions
Refer for a transvaginal ultrasound scan of the pelvis before starting any medical treatment
Commence a non-steroidal anti inflammatory drug started before the pain each cycle
Increase her paracetamol to 1 g four times daily throughout each day of bleeding
Commence a monophasic combined oral contraceptive taken continuously without a break

subtopic_detail: premenopausal woman with spotting between periods and a focal echogenic lesion within the cavity
stem:
You are the general practitioner reviewing a 41-year-old woman with eight months of light spotting that occurs about a week before each period. Her periods themselves remain regular at 30 days and are not heavy, and she has no pain. She has two children, is not using hormonal contraception, and her partner has had a vasectomy.

Her cervical screening test six months ago was negative for oncogenic human papillomavirus, and speculum examination at that visit showed a normal cervix. She has no risk factors for endometrial cancer and her body mass index is 24 kg per square metre. A transvaginal ultrasound arranged at her last visit reports a well defined echogenic lesion measuring 14 mm within the endometrial cavity with a single feeding vessel on colour Doppler, surrounded by normal appearing endometrium. Both ovaries are normal and there is no free fluid. A full blood examination shows haemoglobin 128 g/L (115 to 155).

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Normal cervix on speculum, mobile anteverted uterus of normal size, no adnexal mass
data_table.Imaging: Transvaginal ultrasound: well defined 14 mm echogenic intracavity lesion with a single feeding vessel, normal surrounding endometrium and normal ovaries
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 128 g/L (115 to 155), human papillomavirus testing negative six months ago

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Perform an outpatient endometrial pipelle sampling in the consulting room this afternoon
Repeat the transvaginal ultrasound in the early follicular phase of her next menstrual cycle
Prescribe tranexamic acid during bleeding days and review her symptoms in three months
Refer for hysteroscopic resection of the lesion with the specimen sent for histology
Insert a levonorgestrel releasing intrauterine system to control the intermenstrual spotting

subtopic_detail: woman wanting to conceive with a diffusely enlarged tender uterus and junctional zone thickening
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar seeing a 36-year-old woman referred with worsening period pain and heavy bleeding over three years. She describes a constant dragging heaviness through the whole of the last week of her cycle rather than pain confined to the bleeding days, and she now takes two days off work each month.

She and her partner have been trying to conceive for eleven months. Her cycles are regular at 27 days and she passes clots, but she has never had bleeding between periods. Examination reveals a symmetrically enlarged globular uterus about the size of a ten week pregnancy, which is tender and boggy on bimanual palpation, with no adnexal masses and no nodularity in the pouch of Douglas. Transvaginal ultrasound reports a globular uterus with asymmetrical myometrial wall thickening, junctional zone thickening of 14 mm, and small myometrial cysts. No discrete fibroid is identified and the endometrium and ovaries appear normal.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Symmetrically enlarged globular tender uterus of about ten week size, no adnexal mass, no uterosacral nodularity
data_table.Imaging: Transvaginal ultrasound: globular uterus, asymmetrical myometrial wall thickening, junctional zone 14 mm, myometrial cysts, normal endometrium and ovaries
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 108 g/L (115 to 155), ferritin 14 mcg/L (30 to 200)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management to recommend first?

options.text: Insert a levonorgestrel releasing intrauterine system to reduce bleeding and relieve the pain
Commence a gonadotrophin releasing hormone agonist with add back therapy for six months
Commence iron replacement with tranexamic acid during bleeding and refer to fertility services
Refer for diagnostic laparoscopy with excision of any peritoneal deposits identified
Refer for uterine artery embolisation to reduce both the bleeding and the uterine bulk

subtopic_detail: breastfeeding woman with severe shooting pain and blanching of the nipple starting after the feed ends
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a woman six weeks after the birth of her first baby. She describes severe burning pain in both nipples that comes on a minute or two after the baby comes off the breast and lasts about ten minutes, and she has started dreading feeds. It is much worse when she gets out of the shower or takes the washing off the line on a cold morning.

A lactation consultant reviewed the attachment last week and was satisfied with it, and the baby has regained birth weight and is now gaining 190 g per week. She has completed a course of oral fluconazole and two weeks of topical miconazole prescribed by a colleague, with no improvement. On examination the nipples are intact with no cracks, fissures or discharge, and the areolae and breasts are soft with no erythema, lump or warmth. As you examine her, the tip of the left nipple blanches white, then becomes dusky blue, and then flushes red as the pain she describes builds. She takes no regular medications and has cold hands in winter.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Intact nipples with no fissures, cracks or discharge, soft non erythematous breasts with no palpable lump
data_table.Provoked finding: Triphasic white then blue then red colour change of the nipple tip observed on exposure to room air
data_table.Infant: Regained birth weight, gaining 190 g per week, attachment assessed as satisfactory by a lactation consultant

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Refer her back for further attachment assessment and a review for tongue tie in the infant
Prescribe a longer course of oral fluconazole for her with oral nystatin drops for the baby
Advise warmth immediately after feeds and prescribe oral nifedipine for a two week trial
Advise expressing and cup feeding for two weeks to rest the nipples and allow them to heal
Prescribe oral di flucloxacillin for ten days and advise her to continue feeding from both sides

subtopic_detail: woman unable to tolerate penetration with involuntary tightening and a normal genital examination
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 26-year-old woman who has never been able to have penetrative intercourse. She and her partner of two years have tried many times; she describes a sensation of a wall and involuntary tightening, together with burning at the entrance, and they always stop. She has never been able to insert a tampon and had to abandon an attempted cervical screening test last year.

She is distressed and says she feels she is failing her relationship. She has no history of sexual assault, no dyspareunia beyond the entrance because penetration has never occurred, and no cyclical pelvic pain, bowel or bladder symptoms. On careful inspection with her consent, the vulva looks normal with no fissures, pallor, architectural loss or erythema, and the hymenal ring is patent. Light touch with a cotton bud at the vestibule reproduces her burning and you observe visible contraction of the perineal muscles. She declines any attempt at internal examination and you do not proceed.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Normal vulval architecture with no pallor, fissuring, adhesions or erythema, patent hymenal ring
data_table.Provoked finding: Cotton bud touch at the vestibule reproduces burning with visible involuntary perineal muscle contraction
data_table.History: Lifelong inability to tolerate tampon insertion, cervical screening or penetrative intercourse

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management to recommend?

options.text: Refer to a pelvic floor physiotherapist for graded desensitisation alongside psychosexual therapy
Refer for examination under anaesthesia with division of any obstructing hymenal band
Arrange injection of botulinum toxin into the levator ani muscles under conscious sedation
Prescribe topical oestrogen cream nightly for six weeks and arrange a further review after that
Prescribe topical lidocaine gel for use before intercourse and review her again in three months

subtopic_detail: pregnant childcare worker exposed to a slapped cheek rash outbreak at work in the second trimester
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 31-year-old woman at 16 weeks in her second pregnancy. She works in a childcare centre where three children developed a bright red rash across both cheeks last week, and she has been told to see a doctor. She had face to face contact with all three children in the two days before their rashes appeared.

She feels well and has no rash, fever or joint pains. Her first pregnancy and birth were uncomplicated. Her booking bloods showed her to be rubella immune, varicella immune and negative for syphilis, hepatitis B, hepatitis C and human immunodeficiency virus, and her blood group is O positive. Her 12 week ultrasound was consistent with dates and showed no abnormality. Examination today is unremarkable with a soft non-tender abdomen, a symphysis fundal height consistent with dates, and a fetal heart rate of 148 beats per minute on handheld Doppler.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 84 beats per minute, blood pressure 108/66 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees, fetal heart rate 148 beats per minute
data_table.Examination: Soft non-tender abdomen, symphysis fundal height consistent with dates, no rash or joint swelling
data_table.Booking investigations: Rubella immune, varicella immune, negative syphilis, hepatitis B, hepatitis C and human immunodeficiency virus serology, blood group O positive
data_table.Imaging: Twelve week ultrasound consistent with dates and structurally normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Arrange weekly middle cerebral artery Doppler studies from now until 30 weeks gestation
Reassure her that maternal infection at this gestation carries no risk to the pregnancy
Refer for amniocentesis with viral polymerase chain reaction on the amniotic fluid sample
Offer intravenous immunoglobulin within 72 hours of the exposure to prevent transmission
Send maternal immunoglobulin M and immunoglobulin G serology and act on the result

subtopic_detail: postmenopausal woman with a glazed red vestibule, lacy white streaks and a narrowing vaginal opening
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 58-year-old woman with two years of vulval soreness, a raw burning feeling and a yellow stained discharge. She has been treated with six separate courses of topical and oral antifungal therapy and one course of topical oestrogen without benefit, and intercourse has become impossible.

She went through menopause at 51 and has no other medical problems. She mentions in passing that the inside of her cheeks has been sore and that her dentist commented on some white lines there. On examination the labia minora have partly fused anteriorly and the vaginal opening admits only one fingertip. The vestibule is a glazed bright red with a sharply demarcated edge, and at the margin of the erythema there is a fine lacy white network. There is no white parchment like change over the labia and perineum and no ecchymosis. A vaginal pH is 6.0 and a vaginal swab is negative for candida, bacterial vaginosis and trichomonas.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Glazed sharply demarcated vestibular erythema with a lacy white reticular border, partial anterior labial fusion, introitus admitting one fingertip
data_table.Oral: Reticular white striae on the buccal mucosa with associated soreness
data_table.Investigations: Vaginal pH 6.0, swab negative for candida, bacterial vaginosis and trichomonas

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Prescribe a further eight week course of oral fluconazole taken as a weekly maintenance dose
Refer for surgical division of the adhesions with vaginal dilator therapy started afterwards
Commence an ultrapotent topical corticosteroid for lichen sclerosus and review in three months
Take a punch biopsy from the affected edge and commence long term topical oestrogen therapy
Take a punch biopsy from the affected edge and commence an ultrapotent topical corticosteroid

subtopic_detail: woman who never established milk supply and has had no periods since a delivery needing massive transfusion
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 33-year-old woman nine months after the birth of her second child. She has come about persistent tiredness, feeling cold all the time and dizziness when she stands up quickly. Her periods have not returned and she is using condoms for contraception.

Her delivery was complicated by bleeding requiring eight units of red cells and a return to theatre, and she spent two days in intensive care. She tells you she was never able to produce any milk at all despite considerable support from the lactation service, and that her pubic and axillary hair has thinned. She stopped breastfeeding attempts at three weeks and the baby has thrived on formula. On examination she looks pale with fine dry skin, her blood pressure is 96/58 mmHg lying and 82/50 mmHg standing, her pulse is 64 beats per minute and she is afebrile. Sodium is 128 mmol/L (135 to 145) and a urinary pregnancy test is negative.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 64 beats per minute, blood pressure 96/58 mmHg lying and 82/50 mmHg standing, respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.2 degrees
data_table.Examination: Pale fine dry skin, thinning axillary and pubic hair, no goitre, no hyperpigmentation of palmar creases or buccal mucosa
data_table.Obstetric history: Postpartum haemorrhage requiring eight units of red cells, return to theatre and intensive care admission
data_table.Investigations: Sodium 128 mmol/L (135 to 145), potassium 4.1 mmol/L (3.5 to 5.2), urinary pregnancy test negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Request an early morning cortisol with paired anterior pituitary and thyroid hormone levels
Request a nine item depression questionnaire with thyroid function and vitamin B12 levels
Request a short synacthen test with adrenal antibodies and plasma renin activity
Request a serum prolactin with a follicle stimulating hormone and a transvaginal ultrasound
Request thyroid stimulating hormone alone with a full blood count and iron studies

subtopic_detail: woman whose device threads cannot be seen and whose uterine cavity is empty on transvaginal scanning
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 34-year-old woman who cannot feel the threads of her copper intrauterine device. It was inserted eight months ago at six weeks postpartum while she was fully breastfeeding, and the threads were checked and documented as visible at her six week review after insertion.

Her periods returned four months ago and have been regular since, with no unusually heavy loss and no episode of severe cramping that she recalls. She has had no pelvic pain and no abnormal discharge. A urinary pregnancy test today is negative. On speculum examination no threads are visible at the external os and the cervix looks normal. Gentle exploration of the cervical canal with a thread retriever finds nothing. A transvaginal ultrasound performed in the practice reports an empty uterine cavity with an endometrial thickness of 6 mm, no intrauterine device identified, and normal ovaries with no free fluid.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: No threads visible at the external os, normal cervix, non-tender mobile uterus of normal size
data_table.Imaging: Transvaginal ultrasound: empty uterine cavity, endometrial thickness 6 mm, no device identified, normal ovaries, no free fluid
data_table.Investigations: Urinary pregnancy test negative, insertion at six weeks postpartum during full breastfeeding

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Arrange an outpatient hysteroscopy to inspect the cavity and retrieve the device directly
Refer directly for a diagnostic laparoscopy to locate and retrieve the migrated device
Arrange a transabdominal pelvic ultrasound before considering any further imaging modality
Reassure her that the device has been expelled and reinsert a new device at this visit
Arrange a plain abdominal radiograph covering the diaphragm to the pelvic floor

subtopic_detail: treating on the basis of a minimal trauma fracture when the bone density score is in the osteopenic range
stem:
You are the general practice registrar reviewing a 62-year-old woman six weeks after she tripped on a flat footpath outside the shops and broke her wrist. She fell from standing height onto her outstretched hand and the fracture has been managed in a cast, which has now come off.

Her last menstrual period was at 51. She has never smoked, drinks two standard drinks a week and walks most days. She has never taken oral corticosteroids. Her mother broke her hip at 74. Her body mass index is 22 kg/m2. You arranged a bone density scan and screening bloods after the fracture and the results are now available.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: No thoracic kyphosis, height unchanged from her recorded height five years ago, wrist fracture united with good range of movement
data_table.Investigations: Corrected calcium within normal limits, 25 hydroxyvitamin D within normal limits, thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits, renal function within normal limits, serum protein electrophoresis shows no paraprotein
data_table.Bone densitometry: Femoral neck T score minus 2.3, lumbar spine T score minus 2.1

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Lifestyle advice with a repeat bone density scan in two years
Commence six monthly denosumab injections as initial therapy
Commence menopausal hormone therapy for bone protection alone
Commence an oral bisphosphonate with calcium and vitamin D advice
Commence calcium and vitamin D supplements without other therapy

subtopic_detail: first line medical treatment for heavy painful bleeding with diffuse myometrial changes on ultrasound
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar in the outpatient clinic seeing a 42-year-old woman with three years of periods that have become progressively heavier and more painful. She now floods through a pad hourly on her worst two days and the cramping starts two days before any bleeding appears.

She has had two vaginal births and has not been pregnant for nine years. She has taken over the counter ibuprofen with limited benefit. On bimanual examination the uterus is bulky and globular, about the size of a ten week pregnancy, tender to palpation and mobile, with no separate adnexal mass. Her transvaginal ultrasound and bloods are available.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Uterus bulky and globular at approximately ten week size, tender on bimanual palpation, mobile with no adnexal mass, cervix appears normal
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 104 g/L (115 to 165), ferritin 9 micrograms/L (15 to 200), thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits, cervical screening test up to date and negative
data_table.Imaging: Transvaginal ultrasound shows a globally enlarged uterus with asymmetrical myometrial thickening, small myometrial cysts and an indistinct junctional zone; no discrete fibroid identified; endometrial thickness 6 mm; ovaries normal

lead_in: What would you first recommend as treatment?

options.text: A gonadotrophin releasing hormone agonist with add back therapy
Referral for total hysterectomy at the next available list
A continuous combined oral contraceptive pill regimen
Tranexamic acid taken during the days of heavy bleeding
Insertion of a levonorgestrel releasing intrauterine system

subtopic_detail: initial conservative management of urinary urgency when stress leakage and infection have been excluded
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 58-year-old woman with eight months of a sudden compelling need to pass urine that she struggles to defer. She gets up four times most nights and has twice not made it to the toilet in time.

She tells you she does not leak when she coughs, laughs or lifts her grandchildren, and that the problem is entirely about the urgency. She drinks six cups of coffee across the day and a glass of wine most evenings. She has had two vaginal births and her last period was at 52. She has no haematuria, no dysuria and no pelvic pain. Her examination and investigations are complete.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Mild vaginal atrophy, no prolapse beyond the hymen on Valsalva, no leakage demonstrated on cough stress testing, abdomen soft with no palpable bladder
data_table.Investigations: Urinalysis negative for nitrites and leucocytes, midstream urine culture no growth, post-void residual volume 30 mL on bladder scan, fasting glucose within normal limits, bladder diary shows nine voids by day and four by night with small volumes

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Bladder training with caffeine reduction and pelvic floor exercises
Oral oxybutynin with review of the symptoms in six weeks' time
Oral mirabegron with review of the blood pressure in six weeks
Referral for urodynamic studies before any treatment is started
Referral for insertion of a midurethral sling within three months

subtopic_detail: choosing a drainage technique that reduces recurrence for an acute vulval gland abscess
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar in the emergency department seeing a 27-year-old woman with four days of increasing pain and swelling at the right side of the vaginal opening. The pain has become severe enough that she cannot sit down properly or walk without discomfort and she did not sleep last night.

She has had no fever or rigors and is not pregnant. She has no history of a similar problem. On examination there is a tense tender swelling at the posterior aspect of the right side of the vaginal opening, about 4 cm across, which is fluctuant with thinning of the overlying skin. There is no surrounding spreading redness and no inguinal lymphadenopathy.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 88, blood pressure 118/72, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 99 per cent in air, temperature 36.9 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Tense fluctuant 4 cm swelling at the posterior right introitus with thinned overlying skin, exquisitely tender, no surrounding cellulitis, no inguinal lymphadenopathy, speculum examination deferred because of pain
data_table.Investigations: Urinary beta human chorionic gonadotrophin negative, white cell count within normal limits, C reactive protein mildly raised, sexually transmitted infection screening collected

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Oral antibiotics alone with review in the clinic in three days
Incision and drainage with insertion of a Word catheter
Simple incision and drainage without any further drainage device
Marsupialisation of the cyst in theatre at the next available list
Needle aspiration of the contents under local anaesthetic today

subtopic_detail: addressing a specific factual misunderstanding before referral for a permanent method
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 31-year-old woman who asks to be referred to have her tubes tied. She has three children, the youngest of whom is eight months old, and she and her partner have agreed they do not want more.

She tells you she is certain about her decision and has thought about it since her last pregnancy. When you ask what she understands about the procedure, she says she believes it can be reversed if she changes her mind later, and that she assumed it was done in a clinic room without an anaesthetic. She and her partner currently use condoms and she has not previously used any other method. She has no medical problems and takes no regular medication.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft with a low transverse scar from a previous caesarean birth, no masses, body mass index 27 kg/m2
data_table.Investigations: Cervical screening test up to date and negative, urinary beta human chorionic gonadotrophin negative, haemoglobin within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Insert a levonorgestrel intrauterine system instead of making a referral
Refer directly for laparoscopic tubal occlusion at the next clinic list
Provide counselling on irreversibility and the alternatives before referral
Refer her partner for vasectomy as the lower risk alternative procedure
Decline the request on the grounds of her age and her current parity

subtopic_detail: selecting a uterus conserving procedure after failed medical therapy with a normal cavity and benign histology
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar reviewing a 45-year-old woman with two years of heavy menstrual bleeding. She has two children and had a tubal ligation six years ago.

She took tranexamic acid during her periods for six months with only slight improvement, and a levonorgestrel releasing intrauterine system was inserted last year but she asked for it to be removed after six months because of persistent irregular bleeding that she found unacceptable. Her periods remain heavy but are otherwise regular and there is no bleeding between periods and none after intercourse. Her imaging and endometrial sampling are complete and she asks what can be done next.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Uterus normal size and regular on bimanual palpation, non-tender, cervix appears normal on speculum examination, no adnexal masses
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 108 g/L (115 to 165), ferritin low, thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits, coagulation screen within normal limits, endometrial pipelle biopsy reported as proliferative endometrium with no hyperplasia and no atypia
data_table.Imaging: Transvaginal ultrasound shows a normal sized uterus with endometrial thickness 5 mm, no fibroids and no endometrial polyp, normal ovaries

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next treatment?

options.text: A gonadotrophin releasing hormone agonist for six months
Total hysterectomy with conservation of both ovaries
Reinsertion of a levonorgestrel releasing intrauterine system
Endometrial ablation performed as a day case procedure
Uterine artery embolisation by interventional radiology

subtopic_detail: escalating care when outpatient treatment for pelvic infection has failed and a complex adnexal collection is present
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar in the emergency department assessing a 26-year-old woman with six days of worsening lower abdominal pain and an offensive vaginal discharge. Her general practitioner started oral doxycycline and metronidazole four days ago for pelvic inflammatory disease and she has felt steadily worse since.

She has vomited twice today and has not eaten. She has a copper intrauterine device in place and a new sexual partner in the past three months. She is not pregnant. On bimanual examination there is marked cervical motion tenderness and the right adnexal region is exquisitely tender with a palpable mass. Her ultrasound has been performed in the department.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 118, blood pressure 104/62, respiratory rate 22, SpO2 98 per cent in air, temperature 38.7 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Marked lower abdominal tenderness with guarding in the right iliac fossa, cervical motion tenderness, tender right adnexal mass palpable on bimanual examination, offensive purulent discharge at the cervix
data_table.Investigations: Urinary beta human chorionic gonadotrophin negative, white cell count 19.6 x10^9/L (4.0 to 11.0), C reactive protein 210 mg/L (less than 5), lactate 2.4 mmol/L (0.5 to 2.2), chlamydia and gonorrhoea nucleic acid testing collected
data_table.Imaging: Transvaginal ultrasound shows a 6 cm complex multiloculated right adnexal collection with thick walls and internal debris, free fluid in the pouch of Douglas

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Give intramuscular ceftriaxone and discharge on oral antibiotics
Continue the oral antibiotics and review her again in 48 hours
Proceed to laparotomy with right salpingo oophorectomy today
Arrange image guided drainage as the sole definitive treatment
Admit for intravenous antibiotics with early surgical review

subtopic_detail: localised entry pain with a normal looking vulva after repeated empirical antifungal treatment
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar seeing a 29-year-old woman with fourteen months of burning pain at the entrance to the vagina whenever intercourse is attempted, and the same pain when she tries to insert a tampon. She has no pain at any other time and no pain with deep penetration on the occasions it has been possible.

She has bought four courses of antifungal treatment from the pharmacy over the past year and says none made any difference. She has no abnormal discharge and no itch. She washes with water only and uses no perfumed products. On examination the vulval skin appears entirely normal, with no redness, no fissuring, no whitening and no loss of the normal architecture.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Vulval skin of normal colour and architecture with no erythema, fissures or scarring, gentle cotton bud pressure reproduces sharp burning pain at the posterior vestibule at the five and seven o'clock positions, pelvic floor muscles tender with increased resting tone, speculum examination not attempted
data_table.Investigations: High vaginal swab shows normal flora, candida nucleic acid testing negative, sexually transmitted infection screening negative, urinalysis within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Referral for pelvic floor physiotherapy with education about the condition
A six month course of weekly oral fluconazole with review afterwards
A potent topical corticosteroid ointment applied to the vestibule daily
Referral for surgical vestibulectomy at the next available theatre list
Topical vaginal oestrogen cream applied three nights each week

subtopic_detail: cyclical pain with normal secondary sexual characteristics and an obstructing outflow membrane
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar seeing a 14-year-old girl brought to the emergency department by her mother. For six months she has had lower abdominal pain that comes on about every four weeks and lasts three or four days, and each episode has been worse than the last.

For the past two days she has been unable to pass urine properly and has been going frequently in small amounts. She has never had a period. Her breast development and pubic hair began about three years ago and have progressed normally. On abdominal examination there is a smooth tender mass arising from the pelvis that reaches the umbilicus. On inspecting the external genitalia you see a bulging bluish membrane at the vaginal opening.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 96, blood pressure 112/68, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 99 per cent in air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Breast development Tanner stage 4, pubic hair Tanner stage 4, smooth tender midline suprapubic mass extending to the umbilicus, bulging bluish membrane visible at the introitus with no visible vaginal opening, no inguinal masses
data_table.Investigations: Urinary beta human chorionic gonadotrophin negative, bladder scan shows 480 mL retained urine, creatinine within normal limits, full blood count within normal limits
data_table.Imaging: Pelvic ultrasound shows a markedly distended vagina filled with echogenic fluid, a normal uterus above it and normal ovaries bilaterally

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Karyotype with gonadotrophin and oestradiol levels before any treatment
Surgical incision of the obstructing membrane under general anaesthesia
Magnetic resonance imaging of the pelvis before any intervention is made
A combined oral contraceptive pill to suppress menstruation for now
Needle aspiration of the collection in the clinic under local anaesthetic

subtopic_detail: withholding treatment for midline labial fusion when voiding is unaffected
stem:
You are the paediatric and adolescent gynaecology registrar seeing a 3-year-old girl whose mother noticed while bathing her that the area between the labia appears to have closed over. She is worried that something is badly wrong and that her daughter will need an operation.

The child has no pain and has never had any bleeding or discharge. She was toilet trained six months ago, passes urine in a normal single stream that her mother has watched, and is dry between visits to the toilet. She has never had a urinary tract infection. She is otherwise well and growing normally. On separating the labia majora gently you see the findings recorded below.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Labia minora fused in the midline from the posterior fourchette forwards, with a thin translucent avascular line visible along the fusion, urethral meatus visible at the anterior end of the line, vaginal opening not visible, no erythema, no excoriation, no discharge and no signs of trauma
data_table.Investigations: Urinalysis negative for nitrites and leucocytes, growth parameters tracking along the 50th centile, no investigations otherwise indicated

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Manual separation of the labia in the clinic at today's appointment
Topical oestrogen cream applied to the fused line twice each day
Reassurance with explanation and no active treatment at this stage
Surgical division of the adhesion under a general anaesthetic
Renal tract ultrasound with a referral to paediatric urology

subtopic_detail: managing an incidental cytology finding of filamentous organisms in an asymptomatic device user
stem:
You are the general practice registrar reviewing a 38-year-old woman who has come in for the result of her routine cervical screening test. She has had a copper intrauterine device in place for six years and is happy with it.

The screening result is negative for oncogenic human papillomavirus. The laboratory has added a comment noting the incidental presence of filamentous organisms consistent with actinomyces on the cytology slide. She has no pelvic pain, no change in her discharge, no bleeding between periods and no bleeding after intercourse, and has had no fevers. On examination her abdomen is soft and there is no cervical motion tenderness and no adnexal tenderness or mass.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft and non-tender, cervix appears healthy with device threads visible at the os, no cervical motion tenderness, no adnexal mass or tenderness on bimanual examination
data_table.Investigations: Cervical screening test negative for oncogenic human papillomavirus, cytology reports filamentous organisms consistent with actinomyces as an incidental finding, C reactive protein within normal limits, white cell count within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Leave the device and give two weeks of oral amoxicillin as cover
Remove the intrauterine device and arrange an alternative method
Remove the device and commence a prolonged course of penicillin
Reassure her and leave the device in place without antibiotic treatment
Arrange a pelvic ultrasound before deciding on further management

subtopic_detail: directing a suspicious postmenopausal adnexal mass to the service that should perform the surgery
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar seeing a 56-year-old woman referred by her general practitioner. For three months she has had abdominal bloating, a feeling of fullness after only a few mouthfuls, and a change in her bowel habit, and she was initially told this was likely to be irritable bowel syndrome.

She has lost 4 kg over that period without trying and her skirts no longer do up despite the weight loss. Her last menstrual period was at 50 and she has had no vaginal bleeding since. She has no family history of breast or ovarian cancer. On examination her abdomen is distended with shifting dullness and there is a firm mass palpable arising from the pelvis. Her imaging and tumour marker results are available.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Abdomen distended with shifting dullness, firm irregular mass arising from the pelvis and palpable to just below the umbilicus, no hepatomegaly, no palpable supraclavicular nodes
data_table.Investigations: CA125 480 U/mL (less than 35), haemoglobin 112 g/L (115 to 165), albumin 30 g/L (35 to 50), liver function within normal limits, renal function within normal limits
data_table.Imaging: Transvaginal and abdominal ultrasound show an 8 cm right adnexal mass with solid components and thick irregular septations, a smaller similar left adnexal lesion, and moderate ascites

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Arrange colonoscopy first to exclude a gastrointestinal primary
Repeat the pelvic ultrasound in three months to assess for change
Refer for laparoscopic cystectomy under the general gynaecologist
Repeat the CA125 in six weeks and refer if it continues to rise
Refer to a gynaecological oncology service for further management

subtopic_detail: setting and anaesthesia required once a rectal examination identifies sphincter involvement in a perineal tear
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar called to the birth suite immediately after a spontaneous vaginal birth. The woman is a primigravida who had a prolonged second stage with the baby in the occipito posterior position, and the birth weight was 4.1 kg. No episiotomy was performed.

The midwife asks you to assess the perineum before any repair is started. Inspection shows a tear extending through the perineal skin and the perineal body. You perform a digital rectal examination with the woman's consent and find that the external anal sphincter is torn through less than half of its thickness, while the internal anal sphincter is intact and the rectal mucosa is intact throughout. She has an epidural in situ that is currently providing good analgesia.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 84, blood pressure 118/74, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 99 per cent in air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Perineal tear extending through skin and perineal body, digital rectal examination shows the external anal sphincter torn through less than 50 per cent of its thickness, internal anal sphincter intact, rectal mucosa intact, estimated blood loss 350 mL
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin within normal limits on admission, no coagulopathy, epidural catheter in situ and functioning, baby with the midwife and feeding

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Repair in theatre under regional or general anaesthesia by a trained clinician
Repair in the birth suite using local anaesthetic infiltration now
Repair the perineal body alone and review the sphincter in six weeks
Leave the tear to heal and arrange review in the clinic in six weeks
Refer to the colorectal surgical team for repair at a later date

subtopic_detail: the maternal viral load threshold at which antiviral therapy is added to infant immunoprophylaxis to prevent vertical hepatitis B transmission
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar reviewing a 28-year-old woman at 28 weeks in her first pregnancy. Routine booking bloods showed her to be hepatitis B surface antigen positive, which she had not known about.

Further testing shows she is hepatitis B e antigen positive with a hepatitis B viral load of 2 400 000 IU/mL and normal transaminases. She has no stigmata of chronic liver disease, her liver ultrasound and elastography are normal, and she is not coinfected with hepatitis C, hepatitis D or the human immunodeficiency virus. The pregnancy is otherwise uncomplicated with normal growth and a cephalic presentation. She intends to breastfeed and asks what can be done to protect the baby. She has taken no antiviral treatment before.

data_table.Examination: Symphysis fundal height appropriate for dates, blood pressure 108/66, no hepatomegaly or splenomegaly
data_table.Investigations: Hepatitis B surface antigen positive, e antigen positive, viral load 2 400 000 IU/mL, alanine aminotransferase 24 U/L (less than 35), platelets and coagulation profile within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate additional measure to reduce transmission to her baby?

options.text: Rely on hepatitis B immunoglobulin and vaccine given to the baby at birth
Plan an elective caesarean section at 39 weeks to avoid intrapartum exposure
Advise her to avoid breastfeeding and to use formula from the time of birth
Commence entecavir now and continue it until twelve weeks after the birth
Commence tenofovir disoproxil now and continue it until after she has delivered

subtopic_detail: treating maternal syphilis when the only effective drug is the one that previously caused anaphylaxis
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar seeing a 24-year-old woman at 22 weeks in her second pregnancy. Booking serology has returned a reactive treponemal enzyme immunoassay with a confirmatory particle agglutination assay and a rapid plasma reagin titre of 1 in 32.

She has never been treated for this infection and had a negative test two years ago in her first pregnancy. She recalls no rash, ulcer or illness in the interval. At nineteen she was given amoxicillin for a dental infection and within twenty minutes developed lip and tongue swelling with wheeze, and was treated with intramuscular adrenaline in an emergency department. The morphology scan today shows normal growth, normal liquor volume and no hepatomegaly, ascites or placental thickening. Her partner has been contacted and is being tested.

data_table.Examination: No rash, no mucosal lesion, no lymphadenopathy, symphysis fundal height appropriate for dates
data_table.Investigations: Treponemal enzyme immunoassay reactive, particle agglutination assay reactive, rapid plasma reagin 1 in 32, human immunodeficiency virus and hepatitis serology negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment?

options.text: Oral doxycycline for twenty eight days with repeat serology after completion
Intramuscular ceftriaxone daily for ten days with repeat serology after completion
Penicillin desensitisation in a monitored setting followed by benzathine penicillin
Oral azithromycin as a single dose with repeat serology at four weekly intervals
Defer treatment until after delivery and treat the newborn if serology is positive

subtopic_detail: which antibiotic prolongs latency after preterm prelabour membrane rupture, and which one is avoided because of neonatal bowel injury
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar in the birth suite assessing a 31-year-old woman at 30 weeks and 2 days in her second pregnancy. Three hours ago she felt a sudden gush of clear fluid while getting out of a chair and has been damp since.

A sterile speculum examination shows a pool of clear liquor in the posterior fornix and no cord or fetal part at the cervix. She is having no contractions and her uterus is soft and non-tender. Her vaginal swab for group B streptococcus at 28 weeks was negative. The cardiotocograph shows a baseline of 140 beats per minute with normal variability, accelerations and no decelerations. She has already been given the first dose of an antenatal corticosteroid and has been admitted for inpatient monitoring.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 82, blood pressure 114/70, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 99 per cent in air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius, fetal heart rate 140
data_table.Examination: Clear liquor pooling on speculum, cervix closed on visual inspection, uterus soft and non-tender
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 11.2 x10^9/L (4.0 to 11.0), C reactive protein 6 mg/L (less than 5), high vaginal swab sent

lead_in: Which antibiotic regimen is most appropriate?

options.text: Intravenous benzylpenicillin given only once she is established in labour
Oral erythromycin four times daily for up to ten days or until she labours
Oral amoxicillin with clavulanate three times daily for up to ten days of treatment
Oral metronidazole with clindamycin twice daily for up to ten days of treatment
No antibiotic at present with review if she develops fever or uterine tenderness

subtopic_detail: first line pharmacological ovulation induction in anovulatory subfertility once tubal patency and semen analysis are already known to be normal
stem:
You are the general practitioner with a special interest in women's health seeing a 29-year-old woman who has been trying to conceive for fourteen months. Her periods come every forty five to ninety days and have done so since her teens.

She has noticed coarse dark hair on her chin and along her jaw for several years. Her body mass index is 31 kg/m2 and she has been working with a dietitian and has lost 4 kg over four months without any change to her cycle. Her partner's semen analysis is normal on two separate samples. A hysterosalpingogram performed last month showed both tubes to be patent with free spill. Her thyroid function, prolactin and seventeen hydroxyprogesterone are all normal, and a mid luteal progesterone taken twice was consistent with anovulation.

data_table.Examination: Body mass index 31 kg/m2, terminal hair on the chin and jawline, no acanthosis nigricans, no clitoromegaly
data_table.Investigations: Total testosterone 2.6 nmol/L (0.3 to 1.7), thyroid stimulating hormone, prolactin and seventeen hydroxyprogesterone all within normal limits, pelvic ultrasound shows more than twenty follicles per ovary

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first line pharmacological treatment?

options.text: Metformin as a single agent with review of her cycle pattern after three months
Injectable gonadotrophin therapy with ultrasound monitoring of follicular growth
Referral for in vitro fertilisation given the duration she has been trying to conceive
Clomifene citrate on days two to six of a progestogen induced withdrawal bleed
Letrozole taken for five days early in the cycle with mid luteal progesterone checks

subtopic_detail: how body weight and proximity to ovulation change the choice of emergency contraception thirty eight hours after a condom failure
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 24-year-old woman who tells you a condom broke during sex thirty eight hours ago. She is on day thirteen of a regular twenty eight day cycle.

She weighs 92 kg and her body mass index is 32 kg/m2. She has used condoms alone until now and says she would like something ongoing that she does not have to think about. She has no dysmenorrhoea, no abnormal bleeding and no pelvic pain, and a sexual health screen taken today is pending with no symptoms of infection. She has no history of pelvic inflammatory disease and has never been pregnant. A urine pregnancy test in the clinic is negative and she has had no other unprotected sex this cycle.

data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft and non-tender, no cervical excitation, uterus anteverted and normal size, no adnexal mass
data_table.Investigations: Urine beta human chorionic gonadotropin negative, chlamydia and gonorrhoea nucleic acid testing pending

lead_in: What would you first recommend for emergency contraception?

options.text: Insertion of a copper intrauterine device within the next few days
Levonorgestrel 1.5 mg orally taken as a single dose as soon as possible today
Ulipristal acetate 30 mg orally taken as a single dose as soon as possible today
Levonorgestrel 3 mg orally as a double dose to allow for her higher body weight
Start a combined oral contraceptive today and use condoms for the next seven days

subtopic_detail: ripening an unfavourable cervix at term in a woman with one previous caesarean who wants a vaginal birth
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar in the antenatal day unit seeing a 32-year-old woman at 41 weeks and 0 days in her second pregnancy. Her first baby was born by lower segment caesarean section for a breech presentation at term, with no infection and an uncomplicated recovery.

This pregnancy has been uncomplicated, the fetus is cephalic with an estimated weight on the fiftieth centile, and the placenta is fundal and well clear of the previous scar. She has had no contractions and her membranes are intact. She is clear that she would like to give birth vaginally and has attended two counselling appointments about her options. On vaginal examination the cervix is 1 cm dilated, 1 cm long, firm, posterior and the station is minus three, giving a Bishop score of 3. The cardiotocograph is normal.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78, blood pressure 116/72, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 99 per cent in air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius, fetal heart rate 138
data_table.Examination: Cephalic presentation, Bishop score 3, membranes intact, no uterine tenderness or scar tenderness
data_table.Investigations: Cardiotocograph normal with baseline 138, good variability and accelerations, amniotic fluid index within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate method of induction of labour?

options.text: Transcervical balloon catheter for ripening, then amniotomy and oxytocin
Vaginal prostaglandin E2 gel repeated after six hours, then amniotomy and oxytocin
Vaginal misoprostol in low dose repeated six hourly, then amniotomy and oxytocin
Amniotomy today followed by an oxytocin infusion titrated to contraction frequency
Elective repeat caesarean section arranged for tomorrow given her unfavourable cervix

subtopic_detail: what to do with a treated hypothyroid woman's replacement dose on the day she reports a positive pregnancy test
stem:
You are the general practitioner taking a telephone call from a 30-year-old woman who has just had a positive home pregnancy test. Her last menstrual period was five weeks ago and the pregnancy was planned.

She has autoimmune hypothyroidism diagnosed six years ago with positive thyroid peroxidase antibodies, and has taken levothyroxine 100 micrograms daily without missing doses. Her thyroid function was checked three months ago as part of her preconception care and her thyroid stimulating hormone was 2.0 mIU/L with a normal free thyroxine. She takes no other medication, no iron and no calcium supplement, and takes her tablet on an empty stomach each morning. She has no goitre, no palpitations and no heat intolerance. She asks whether she should change anything now or wait until her first antenatal appointment in three weeks.

data_table.Examination: Not examined; telephone consultation
data_table.Investigations: Thyroid stimulating hormone 2.0 mIU/L (0.4 to 4.0) and free thyroxine within normal limits three months ago

lead_in: What is the most appropriate advice to give her today?

options.text: Continue the same daily dose and have thyroid function checked at twelve weeks
Take two extra tablets each week from today and check thyroid function in four weeks
Arrange thyroid function testing today and adjust the dose once the result arrives
Reduce the daily dose slightly to allow for the pregnancy related rise in hormone
Add liothyronine to her current regimen and check thyroid function in four weeks

subtopic_detail: a seizure free woman on valproate who wants to conceive within the year, and whether folate supplementation is sufficient mitigation
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 27-year-old teacher who tells you she and her partner would like to start trying for a baby in the next few months. She has generalised tonic clonic seizures that began at fourteen.

She has taken sodium valproate 1000 mg daily for six years and has been free of seizures for the past three. She holds an unrestricted driver licence. She currently uses a copper intrauterine device for contraception. She has not seen her neurologist for two years because she has been well. She has no other medical conditions, takes no other medication, and there is no family history of neural tube defect. She asks whether she should simply start folic acid and continue as she is.

data_table.Examination: Neurological examination normal, blood pressure 112/70, body mass index 24 kg/m2
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, urea electrolytes and creatinine and liver function tests all within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Continue valproate at the current dose and add folic acid 5 mg daily now
Continue valproate and arrange an early detailed morphology scan once she conceives
Refer urgently to neurology to plan a change of medication before she conceives
Stop the valproate now and review her seizure control again in three months
Change her today to carbamazepine at an equivalent dose and review in one month

subtopic_detail: epigastric pain with falling platelets and rising transaminases at thirty four weeks when the blood pressure is only mildly raised
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar assessing a 34-year-old woman at 34 weeks and 3 days in her first pregnancy who came in overnight with twelve hours of pain under her ribs on the right and persistent nausea. She thought she had eaten something that disagreed with her.

She has no headache, no visual disturbance and no ankle swelling that she has noticed. Her blood pressure at her last antenatal visit a week ago was 118 over 72 with no proteinuria. She has vomited twice. Her blood glucose is normal and she is not confused or drowsy. Fetal movements have been normal and the cardiotocograph is reassuring. She takes no regular medication and has had no previous liver or gallbladder problems.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 96, blood pressure 148/94, respiratory rate 18, SpO2 98 per cent in air, temperature 36.9 degrees Celsius, fetal heart rate 145
data_table.Examination: Tender in the right upper quadrant and epigastrium, no guarding, reflexes normal with no clonus, uterus soft and non-tender
data_table.Investigations: Platelets 78 x10^9/L (150 to 400), alanine aminotransferase 210 U/L (less than 35), lactate dehydrogenase 720 U/L (120 to 250), haptoglobin low, blood film shows fragmented red cells, creatinine 62 micromol/L (45 to 90), international normalised ratio 1.0, glucose 5.1 mmol/L, urine protein creatinine ratio 38 mg/mmol (less than 30)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Transfuse platelets and repeat the full blood count before deciding on delivery
Manage expectantly with twice weekly bloods and birth planned at 37 weeks
Give dexamethasone to raise the platelet count and continue the pregnancy further
Commence magnesium sulfate and antihypertensive therapy, and plan birth today
Start oral labetalol and arrange outpatient review with repeat bloods in two days

subtopic_detail: first trimester anticoagulation for a mechanical mitral prosthesis where the daily warfarin requirement sits at the embryopathy dose threshold
stem:
You are the obstetric medicine registrar seeing a 31-year-old woman who had a bileaflet mechanical mitral valve replacement at twenty four for rheumatic heart disease. She had a positive pregnancy test three days ago and is now six weeks by her dates.

She takes warfarin 4 mg daily with a target international normalised ratio of 2.5 to 3.5 and her results have been within range at every check for two years. She has had no thromboembolic event and no bleeding. Her echocardiogram four months ago showed a normally functioning prosthesis with no pannus, no regurgitation and a normal left atrial size, and she is in sinus rhythm. She has no other medical conditions and takes no other medication. She has read online that warfarin harms babies and has already missed two doses because she was frightened to take it.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 76 and regular, blood pressure 110/68, respiratory rate 14, SpO2 99 per cent in air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Crisp mechanical first heart sound, no murmur of prosthetic dysfunction, chest clear, no peripheral oedema
data_table.Investigations: International normalised ratio 1.6 today, full blood count and creatinine within normal limits, transthoracic echocardiogram four months ago showed normal prosthetic function

lead_in: What is the most appropriate anticoagulation plan for the first trimester?

options.text: Switch to a direct oral anticoagulant for the first trimester, then resume warfarin
Withhold anticoagulation until twelve weeks, then restart warfarin at her usual dose
Switch to twice daily therapeutic enoxaparin with dosing guided by her weight alone
Switch to a continuous unfractionated heparin infusion for the whole first trimester
Restore warfarin at her usual dose now with close monitoring after documented counselling

subtopic_detail: advising about feeding and antibiotics for a painful red breast segment with fever in the third postnatal week
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 29-year-old woman who is 18 days postnatal after an uncomplicated vaginal birth of her first baby, and who has been exclusively breastfeeding.

She has had 36 hours of aching and shivering and feels as though she has influenza. A wedge shaped area of her left breast is red, hot and painful, and feeding from that side is uncomfortable. She has had cracked nipples since the first week and has been feeding the baby mostly on the right because the left hurts. There is no discrete lump that moves under your fingers, no fluctuance and no overlying skin breakdown. The baby is feeding well, has plenty of wet nappies and is back above birth weight. She asks whether she should stop feeding from that breast.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 102/min, blood pressure 112/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 38.6 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Wedge shaped erythema over the upper outer quadrant of the left breast with warmth and tenderness, generalised firmness of that segment, no fluctuant mass, no axillary abscess, fissured left nipple, right breast normal
data_table.Investigations: None performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Stop feeding from the affected breast and suppress lactation on that side
Arrange urgent breast ultrasound and surgical referral for drainage of an abscess
Advise cold packs and simple analgesia alone with review only if she worsens
Prescribe oral metronidazole and advise expressing and discarding the milk
Continue feeding from both breasts with oral flucloxacillin and feeding review

subtopic_detail: deciding whether an incidental late pregnancy platelet fall needs treatment or only observation
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar reviewing a 27-year-old woman at 34 weeks in her first pregnancy whose routine full blood count shows a platelet count of 98 x10^9/L.

She feels entirely well. She has had no bruising, no bleeding from her gums, no nosebleeds and no petechiae. Her platelet count was 243 x10^9/L at booking and 176 x10^9/L at 28 weeks. She has no history of autoimmune disease, takes no medication and has never had a low platelet count outside pregnancy. Her blood pressure has been normal at every visit and her urinalysis today shows no protein. Her liver enzymes, creatinine and urate are all within normal limits, and her blood film shows no fragments, no clumping and no atypical cells. She is anxious about whether she can have an epidural.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 82/min, blood pressure 114/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C, fetal heart rate 142/min
data_table.Examination: No bruising, petechiae or mucosal bleeding, no hepatosplenomegaly, no oedema, no epigastric or right upper quadrant tenderness, symphysiofundal height 34 cm
data_table.Investigations: Platelets 98 x10^9/L (150-400), haemoglobin 118 g/L (110-140), alanine aminotransferase and bilirubin within normal limits, creatinine 58 micromol/L (45-90), urate within normal limits for gestation, blood film shows no fragments or platelet clumping, urinalysis negative for protein

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Commence oral prednisolone to raise the count before she reaches term
Give intravenous immunoglobulin now and repeat the count in 48 hours
Repeat the count at intervals through to delivery with no specific treatment
Deliver her within 24 hours after administering antenatal corticosteroids
Transfuse platelets before labour to ensure a safe count for regional anaesthesia

subtopic_detail: adjusting thyroid hormone replacement at the moment a treated hypothyroid woman confirms she is pregnant
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 30-year-old woman who has just had a positive home pregnancy test. Her last menstrual period was six weeks ago and a serum test today confirms the pregnancy.

She has had Hashimoto thyroiditis for eight years and takes levothyroxine 100 micrograms daily. Her thyroid stimulating hormone three months ago was 2.9 mIU/L, which her previous doctor described as satisfactory. She feels well, has no goitre symptoms and has had no change in weight, bowel habit or heat tolerance. She takes an over the counter pregnancy multivitamin containing iron and calcium with her breakfast, at the same time as her levothyroxine tablet. She asks whether she needs to change anything.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 76/min, blood pressure 106/64 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C
data_table.Examination: No goitre palpable, no tremor, no lid lag, reflexes normal with a normal relaxation phase, no pretibial change
data_table.Investigations: Thyroid stimulating hormone 2.9 mIU/L three months ago on current dose, thyroid peroxidase antibodies strongly positive at diagnosis, beta human chorionic gonadotrophin consistent with six weeks gestation

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management today?

options.text: Continue the current dose and recheck thyroid function at 20 weeks gestation
Stop levothyroxine now and retest thyroid function in four weeks' time
Add liothyronine to the current levothyroxine and test again in six weeks
Increase the levothyroxine dose now and separate it from the multivitamin
Measure free triiodothyronine and adjust the dose according to that result

subtopic_detail: planning surveillance after evacuation of a complete molar pregnancy in a woman who wants to conceive again soon
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar reviewing a 31-year-old woman two weeks after suction evacuation of the uterus. She had presented at 11 weeks with vaginal bleeding and a uterus larger than expected for dates, with hyperemesis requiring admission.

Her pre-evacuation human chorionic gonadotrophin was 268 000 IU/L and her ultrasound had shown a heterogeneous intrauterine mass with multiple small cystic spaces and no fetal parts. Histopathology reports diffuse trophoblastic hyperplasia with hydropic villi and absent fetal tissue. Her bleeding has settled and she feels well. Her human chorionic gonadotrophin today is 4 100 IU/L. She and her partner are keen to try for another pregnancy as soon as possible and she asks whether she should stop using contraception now.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 78/min, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 15/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft and non-tender, uterus no longer palpable abdominally, minimal vaginal bleeding, no adnexal mass, chest clear
data_table.Investigations: Human chorionic gonadotrophin 268 000 IU/L before evacuation and 4 100 IU/L today, histopathology confirms diffuse trophoblastic hyperplasia with hydropic villi and no fetal tissue, haemoglobin 116 g/L (115-155), thyroid function within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate advice about follow up and future pregnancy?

options.text: Begin methotrexate now because the hormone level remains substantially raised
Repeat the evacuation to ensure that no residual molar tissue has been retained
Serial hormone surveillance with reliable contraception until follow up completes
Advise that no follow up is required now that the uterus has been emptied
Recommend hysterectomy given the very high pre-evacuation hormone concentration

subtopic_detail: planning mode of birth after a first episode of genital ulceration acquired close to term
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar seeing a 26-year-old woman at 36 weeks in her first pregnancy who presents with three days of painful vulval ulceration, dysuria and feeling generally unwell.

She describes a cluster of small blisters that broke down into shallow painful ulcers, and she has tender swollen glands in both groins. She has never had anything like this before and has had no previous genital or oral ulceration of any kind. Her partner has recently disclosed a past episode of genital blistering. A swab from the ulcer base has returned positive for herpes simplex virus type 2 by polymerase chain reaction, and type specific serology taken the same day shows no herpes simplex virus type 1 or type 2 antibodies. She has had no contractions and no ruptured membranes.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 92/min, blood pressure 112/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 17/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 37.8 degrees C, fetal heart rate 148/min
data_table.Examination: Multiple shallow tender vulval ulcers with surrounding erythema, bilateral tender inguinal lymphadenopathy, cervix closed on speculum with no ruptured membranes, symphysiofundal height 36 cm
data_table.Investigations: Ulcer swab positive for herpes simplex virus type 2 by polymerase chain reaction, type specific serology negative for both type 1 and type 2 antibodies, syphilis and human immunodeficiency virus serology negative, full blood count within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Plan vaginal birth with intrapartum aciclovir given to the mother in labour
Treat the episode topically and reassess the need for caesarean only in labour
Perform serial viral swabs from 38 weeks and allow vaginal birth if they are negative
Start oral aciclovir now and offer caesarean section at term for this birth
Give the neonate prophylactic aciclovir after a planned vaginal birth at term

subtopic_detail: responding to a woman who has halved her preventer dose in early pregnancy because she is worried about the baby
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 26-year-old woman at 14 weeks in her first pregnancy for a routine antenatal visit. She has had asthma since childhood and was well controlled before pregnancy on budesonide with formoterol as a combination preventer taken twice daily.

She tells you that when she found out she was pregnant she halved her preventer because she did not want the baby exposed to a steroid. Since then she has needed her salbutamol most days, has woken breathless twice in the past week and has stopped walking the dog up the hill near her house. She has had no fever, no coloured sputum and no chest pain. She has not smoked and there is no hay fever flare. Her peak expiratory flow today is 300 L/min against a personal best of 450 L/min.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 88/min, blood pressure 104/64 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C, fetal heart rate 150/min
data_table.Examination: Speaking in full sentences, mild expiratory wheeze throughout both lung fields, no accessory muscle use, no focal crackles
data_table.Investigations: Peak expiratory flow 300 L/min against a personal best of 450 L/min, no other investigations performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Restore the preventer to her pre-pregnancy dose and review in two weeks
Stop the preventer entirely and use salbutamol whenever she has symptoms
Add montelukast in place of restoring the inhaled corticosteroid dose
Prescribe a two week course of oral prednisolone and continue the halved dose
Arrange a chest radiograph and spirometry before altering any of her treatment

subtopic_detail: recognising anterior pituitary failure when lactation never establishes after a major obstetric haemorrhage
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 32-year-old woman ten weeks after the birth of her second child. Her delivery was complicated by a postpartum haemorrhage of 3 200 mL requiring six units of red cells and a period of hypotension in the operating theatre.

She tells you she was never able to produce enough milk despite persistent effort with a lactation consultant, and gave up at four weeks. She has had no periods since the birth, feels exhausted, is cold all the time and has become dizzy on standing. She has no headache and no visual disturbance. She is not breastfeeding now and a pregnancy test is negative. Her thyroid stimulating hormone is 0.8 mIU/L with a free thyroxine of 7 pmol/L, her 9 am cortisol is 62 nmol/L, and her prolactin is below the detection limit of the assay.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 92/min, blood pressure 96/60 mmHg lying and 82/54 mmHg standing, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.2 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Pallor with dry skin, loss of axillary and pubic hair, no goitre, visual fields full to confrontation, no galactorrhoea, breasts soft and non engorged
data_table.Investigations: Thyroid stimulating hormone 0.8 mIU/L (0.4-4.0) with free thyroxine 7 pmol/L (10-20), 9 am cortisol 62 nmol/L (200-700), prolactin undetectable, sodium 129 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 4.2 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), beta human chorionic gonadotrophin negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Replace hydrocortisone first, then thyroxine, and image the pituitary
Start levothyroxine now and review her thyroid function again in six weeks
Reassure her that amenorrhoea and fatigue are expected in the postnatal period
Commence the combined oral contraceptive pill to restore her menstrual cycle
Measure thyroid autoantibodies and treat this as postpartum thyroiditis instead

subtopic_detail: responding to a thickened plaque arising within long standing white atrophic vulval skin
stem:
You are the gynaecologist reviewing a 64-year-old woman who has had vulval itching for nine years, diagnosed as lichen sclerosus on biopsy six years ago and controlled with an ultrapotent topical corticosteroid used intermittently.

She has attended today because one area now feels different. Over the past four months a firm raised area has developed on the right labium majus, and it has not changed despite eight weeks of daily ultrapotent topical corticosteroid, which had always settled her symptoms before. She has no vaginal bleeding and no discharge. Her cervical screening history is complete and normal, and she has never smoked. On examination the vulval skin is generally pale, thinned and crinkled with loss of the labia minora and narrowing of the introitus, and within that skin there is a 15 mm firm indurated plaque on the right labium majus.

data_table.Examination: Generalised vulval pallor with thinned crinkled skin, resorption of the labia minora, introital narrowing, a discrete 15 mm firm indurated plaque on the right labium majus with an intact surface, no inguinal lymphadenopathy
data_table.Investigations: Vulval swab negative for candida and bacterial pathogens, previous vulval biopsy six years ago confirmed lichen sclerosus

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Escalate to a topical calcineurin inhibitor applied twice daily for three months
Biopsy the thickened area to exclude vulval intraepithelial neoplasia
Reassure her that this represents hypertrophic disease and review in six months
Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the pelvis and groins before any biopsy
Refer for wide local excision of the entire affected vulval skin without biopsy

subtopic_detail: deciding whether to attempt instrumental birth in the room or move to theatre when the head is not as low as the caput suggests
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar called to a birth suite for a 28-year-old woman in her first pregnancy at 40 weeks. She has been pushing for two hours with an epidural in place and is becoming exhausted.

The cardiotocograph shows a baseline of 150 beats per minute with variable decelerations to 90 recovering within a minute, and normal variability. On abdominal palpation two fifths of the head is palpable above the pubic symphysis. On vaginal examination the cervix is fully dilated, the head is in the right occipitotransverse position, there is 3 plus caput and 2 plus moulding, and the presenting part feels to be at the level of the ischial spines. The liquor is clear. The birth suite is adjacent to the operating theatre and an anaesthetist is present in the unit.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 96/min, blood pressure 118/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 37.0 degrees C, fetal heart rate 150/min
data_table.Examination: Two fifths of the head palpable abdominally, cervix fully dilated, right occipitotransverse position, station at the ischial spines, caput 3 plus, moulding 2 plus, clear liquor, effective epidural in place
data_table.Investigations: Cardiotocograph baseline 150/min with normal variability and variable decelerations to 90/min recovering within one minute

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Apply non rotational forceps in the room and deliver in the current position
Continue pushing for a further hour with oxytocin augmentation commenced
Move to theatre for a trial of instrumental birth with immediate recourse to caesarean
Perform an immediate category one caesarean section without any vaginal attempt
Attempt manual rotation and vacuum extraction in the room with paediatric support

subtopic_detail: selecting bone protection in a recently menopausal woman with troublesome flushes and an intact uterus
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 53-year-old woman whose last menstrual period was two years ago. She has twelve to fifteen hot flushes a day and wakes drenched most nights, and she has stopped attending her book club because of them.

Her mother fractured a hip at 70. She is a lifelong non smoker, drinks two standard drinks a week and walks daily. She has an intact uterus, has never had a venous thrombosis, has no personal or family history of breast cancer and her mammogram last month was normal. Her blood pressure is 118/74 mmHg and her body mass index is 24 kg/m2. A bone mineral density scan performed because of her family history shows a lumbar spine T score of minus 2.1 and a femoral neck T score of minus 1.9, and she has had no fractures. Her calcium, vitamin D and thyroid function are all normal.

data_table.Examination: Body mass index 24 kg/m2, blood pressure 118/74 mmHg, no breast masses, no spinal tenderness, height unchanged from her recorded height at age 40
