data_table.Investigations: Lumbar spine T score minus 2.1, femoral neck T score minus 1.9, corrected calcium 2.35 mmol/L (2.10-2.60), 25 hydroxyvitamin D 78 nmol/L (50-150), thyroid stimulating hormone 2.1 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), mammogram normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first line treatment?

options.text: Oral alendronate weekly with calcium and vitamin D supplementation added
Combined oestrogen and progestogen menopausal hormone therapy
Transdermal oestradiol used alone without any additional endometrial protection
Denosumab by subcutaneous injection every six months with calcium monitoring
Venlafaxine at a low dose with weight bearing exercise and dietary calcium advice

subtopic_detail: a visible cervical abnormality that must not be accepted as the cause of bleeding without exclusion
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 23-year-old woman with three months of spotting after intercourse and occasional light bleeding between periods. She started the combined oral contraceptive pill five months ago and takes it reliably at the same time each day.

She has a new partner of four months and they use the pill alone for contraception. She has no pelvic pain, no discharge that she has noticed, no fevers and no weight loss. Her only cervical screening test was two years ago and reported no oncogenic human papillomavirus. On speculum examination there is a symmetrical ring of red velvety tissue extending from the external os onto the surrounding cervix, which bleeds lightly when touched by the swab. The uterus is normal sized and mobile with no adnexal mass or cervical motion tenderness.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Symmetrical circumferential red velvety area around the external os bleeding on contact, no ulceration, no irregular mass, uterus normal size and mobile, no adnexal mass or cervical motion tenderness
data_table.Investigations: Cervical screening two years ago negative for oncogenic human papillomavirus, pregnancy test negative today
data_table.Medications: Combined oral contraceptive pill containing 30 micrograms of ethinylestradiol

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Take endocervical and vaginal swabs for chlamydia and gonorrhoea before attributing the bleeding
Refer for colposcopy because contact bleeding requires exclusion of cervical malignancy
Reassure her that the appearance is benign and review her only if the bleeding persists
Perform cervical screening today, since a test more than twelve months old is unreliable
Change to a pill containing 20 micrograms of ethinylestradiol to settle the bleeding

subtopic_detail: whether immunoglobulin is owed for first trimester bleeding with a viable intrauterine pregnancy
stem:
You are the resident in the early pregnancy assessment service seeing a 29-year-old woman in her first pregnancy at 9 weeks and 2 days with two days of light red spotting that needed a liner but not a pad. The bleeding has now stopped.

She has mild lower abdominal cramping that she rates 2 out of 10, no shoulder tip pain, no dizziness and no passage of tissue. She has had no procedures in this pregnancy, no trauma and no abdominal injury. Her booking bloods show blood group O rhesus D negative with a negative antibody screen. Transvaginal ultrasound today shows a single intrauterine gestation with a crown rump length matching dates, cardiac activity present, and a small subchorionic haematoma. Her cervix is closed on speculum examination.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 78/min, blood pressure 112/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft with mild suprapubic tenderness, cervical os closed, minimal old blood in the vault, no adnexal mass
data_table.Investigations: Blood group O rhesus D negative, antibody screen negative, haemoglobin 128 g/L (115-155), ultrasound viable intrauterine pregnancy with small subchorionic haematoma

lead_in: What should you do about her rhesus status?

options.text: Send a Kleihauer test and give immunoglobulin only if fetomaternal haemorrhage is shown
Give 250 IU of anti D immunoglobulin today because she has bled in this pregnancy
Give 625 IU of anti D immunoglobulin today and repeat the antibody screen in six weeks
Arrange cell free fetal DNA typing to establish the fetal rhesus group before deciding
Give no immunoglobulin now and arrange the routine dose in the third trimester

subtopic_detail: counselling on mode of birth after a repaired anal sphincter injury in a woman with no continence symptoms
stem:
You are the registrar in the antenatal clinic seeing a 31-year-old woman at 30 weeks in her second pregnancy. Her first birth was a forceps delivery with a third degree tear repaired in theatre by a consultant, and she asks whether she should have a caesarean this time.

She has no leakage of wind or stool, no urgency and no soiling, and she says her bowel control feels the same as it did before her first baby. She had physiotherapy for six months afterwards and completes pelvic floor exercises most days. Anorectal manometry and endoanal ultrasound arranged by the perineal clinic eighteen months ago were reported as normal. This pregnancy has been uncomplicated, the fetus is cephalic with growth on the 55th centile, and the estimated fetal weight is similar to her first baby.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Symphysis fundal height 30 cm, cephalic presentation, fetal heart rate 142/min, perineum well healed with no scarring tenderness
data_table.Investigations: Anorectal manometry and endoanal ultrasound normal eighteen months ago, growth scan estimated fetal weight on the 55th centile

lead_in: What would you advise her about mode of birth?

options.text: Support a planned vaginal birth, noting her normal symptoms and normal investigations
Recommend vaginal birth with a routine episiotomy performed to protect the sphincter
Plan vaginal birth but avoid instrumental delivery by proceeding directly to caesarean
Repeat the anorectal manometry and endoanal ultrasound before making any recommendation
Recommend an elective caesarean because any previous sphincter injury makes it safer

subtopic_detail: setting the timing of birth in twins according to the chorionicity determined in the first trimester
stem:
You are the registrar seeing a 33-year-old woman at 32 weeks in a twin pregnancy conceived after in vitro fertilisation with two embryos transferred. She asks when her babies will be born and whether she needs a caesarean.

The dating scan at 12 weeks showed two separate placental masses with a thick dividing membrane and a lambda sign at the base. Growth scans every four weeks have shown both twins tracking on the 40th and 50th centiles with normal umbilical artery Doppler studies and normal liquor volumes. Her blood pressure has been normal throughout, her oral glucose tolerance test was normal, and she has had no bleeding, contractions or ruptured membranes. Twin one is cephalic and twin two is transverse today.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 88/min, blood pressure 118/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Uterus large for dates as expected, twin one cephalic, twin two transverse, no uterine tenderness or contractions
data_table.Investigations: Dating scan lambda sign with two placental masses, growth scans both twins on the 40th and 50th centiles, normal umbilical artery Doppler studies, haemoglobin 108 g/L (110-140)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate plan for timing of birth?

options.text: Plan birth at 37 to 38 weeks and decide the mode closer to the time
Plan birth at 36 to 37 weeks because of the risk of unexpected loss in twin pregnancy
Continue to 40 weeks with twice weekly monitoring as for any uncomplicated pregnancy
Plan an elective caesarean at 34 weeks with corticosteroids because twin two is transverse
Plan birth at 32 to 34 weeks given the low haemoglobin and the twin pregnancy

subtopic_detail: choosing between uterine sparing procedures when future pregnancy is intended
stem:
You are the registrar in the gynaecology clinic seeing a 34-year-old woman with two years of increasing pelvic pressure, urinary frequency and a sensation of fullness in her lower abdomen. She and her partner intend to start trying to conceive next year.

Her periods are regular and moderately heavy but her haemoglobin is normal. She has no postcoital or intermenstrual bleeding. Examination reveals a firm irregular mass arising from the pelvis reaching to just below the umbilicus. Transvaginal and abdominal ultrasound shows a 9 cm intramural fibroid on the anterior uterine wall indenting the bladder, with a normal endometrial cavity and normal ovaries. Her cervical screening is up to date and normal.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Firm irregular pelvic mass palpable to just below the umbilicus, mobile, non-tender, cervix normal on speculum
data_table.Investigations: Ultrasound 9 cm anterior intramural fibroid indenting the bladder, endometrial cavity normal, ovaries normal, haemoglobin 131 g/L (115-155)

lead_in: Which treatment should you recommend?

options.text: Arrange magnetic resonance imaging to exclude malignancy before any treatment is offered
Insert a levonorgestrel releasing intrauterine device to control her symptoms medically
Refer for uterine artery embolisation as a less invasive way to shrink the fibroid
Start a gonadotropin releasing hormone agonist for six months to shrink the fibroid
Refer for myomectomy with counselling about uterine scar risks in a future labour

subtopic_detail: the sequence of assessment after a first report of reduced movements in the third trimester
stem:
You are the midwife coordinator's registrar receiving a 26-year-old woman at 32 weeks and 4 days in her first pregnancy who telephoned the assessment unit because her baby has been moving less since yesterday afternoon. She has come in immediately as advised.

She describes the movements as fewer and weaker rather than absent, and she has felt three movements in the past hour while sitting quietly. She has had no bleeding, no abdominal pain, no fluid loss and no itching. Her pregnancy has been uncomplicated, her blood pressure has been normal at every visit and her morphology scan was normal. She smokes three cigarettes a day. On abdominal palpation the uterus is soft and non-tender, the presentation is cephalic, and the symphysis fundal height measures 29 cm having been 30 cm two weeks ago.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 82/min, blood pressure 114/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees C, fetal heart rate 145/min on auscultation
data_table.Examination: Uterus soft and non-tender, cephalic presentation, symphysis fundal height 29 cm at 32 weeks and 4 days, no vaginal loss on inspection
data_table.Investigations: None performed since arrival

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Give corticosteroids and admit her for continuous monitoring until the movements return
Ask her to drink cold water, lie on her side and count movements for two hours
Arrange a biophysical profile as the single assessment and omit the cardiotocograph
Perform cardiotocography and discharge her home if the trace is normal with advice
Perform cardiotocography now and arrange a growth scan with umbilical artery Doppler

subtopic_detail: contraceptive choice when the reliability of an oral method is compromised by altered gut anatomy
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 31-year-old woman eight weeks after a Roux en Y gastric bypass. She has lost 14 kg and wants contraception, having been told by the surgical team to avoid pregnancy for the first eighteen months while her weight is changing rapidly.

She has two children, both born vaginally, and does not want more for at least three years. Her periods are regular and not heavy. She has no history of venous thromboembolism, no migraine of any kind, and she does not smoke. Her blood pressure today is 118/74 mmHg and her current body mass index is 38. She asks whether she can simply restart the combined pill she used before the operation, since she got on well with it.

data_table.Vital signs: Blood pressure 118/74 mmHg, pulse rate 72/min, other observations within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Body mass index 38, abdominal wounds healed, no calf tenderness or swelling, no goitre
data_table.Investigations: Pregnancy test negative, haemoglobin 124 g/L (115-155), full blood count otherwise normal
data_table.Medications: Colecalciferol, a multivitamin and oral iron as prescribed after surgery

lead_in: What contraception should you recommend?

options.text: Condoms alone, since hormonal methods are less effective at a body mass index of 38
Restart the combined oral contraceptive pill she used successfully before the operation
An intrauterine device or the contraceptive implant, avoiding oral methods altogether
The contraceptive vaginal ring, changed monthly, as an effective non oral hormonal option
A progestogen only pill taken at the same time each day with a written reminder

subtopic_detail: prepregnancy planning where the supplement dose and the medicine itself both need to change
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 26-year-old woman who has been seizure free for three years on sodium valproate 800 mg twice daily for generalised epilepsy. She has stopped her contraceptive pill and says she and her husband want to start trying to conceive in the next couple of months.

She takes no other medication and has no other medical problems. She has read online that women planning pregnancy should take folic acid and has bought a supermarket multivitamin containing 500 micrograms of folic acid. She is otherwise well, her weight is stable with a body mass index of 24, and she has no family history of neural tube defects. She has not yet seen her neurologist about the pregnancy plan.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Body mass index 24, neurological examination normal, no rash or gum hypertrophy
data_table.Investigations: None performed
data_table.Medications: Sodium valproate 800 mg twice daily, multivitamin containing folic acid 500 micrograms daily

lead_in: What is the most appropriate advice at this visit?

options.text: Continue the current dose because three years seizure free makes a change too risky
Stop the valproate today and recheck her in four weeks to confirm she remains well
Advise continuing contraception and arrange urgent neurology review to change her medicine
Refer for detailed fetal morphology imaging once she conceives and change nothing now
Increase her folic acid to 5 mg daily and tell her she can start trying immediately

subtopic_detail: which investigations to order first when a couple has been trying for a year with regular cycles
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a couple who have been having regular unprotected intercourse for fourteen months without conceiving. She is 29, he is 31, and neither has children.

Her cycles are regular at 29 days with three days of moderate bleeding, no severe period pain and no pain with intercourse. She has never had pelvic inflammatory disease, abdominal surgery or an abnormal cervical screening result, and her body mass index is 23. He has no history of mumps orchitis, testicular surgery, undescended testis or chemotherapy, and he does not use anabolic steroids. Neither smokes. Her rubella serology from a previous visit shows immunity and she has been taking folic acid for three months.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Body mass index 23, normal secondary sexual characteristics, no hirsutism, abdominal and pelvic examination unremarkable
data_table.Investigations: Rubella immune, cervical screening normal twelve months ago, no fertility investigations performed

lead_in: Which investigations should you arrange first?

options.text: Diagnostic laparoscopy with dye studies to assess tubal patency and pelvic disease
Semen analysis for him and a mid luteal progesterone for her with chlamydia testing
Advise timed intercourse with ovulation prediction kits and review again in six months
Anti Mullerian hormone with a day 3 follicle stimulating hormone and oestradiol for her
Hysterosalpingogram now and referral to a fertility specialist for a treatment cycle

subtopic_detail: the headache feature that makes combined hormonal contraception unacceptable rather than merely cautious
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 24-year-old woman who wants to start the combined oral contraceptive pill because her friend found it helped her skin. She has no children and does not want to conceive for several years.

She describes headaches about once a month, each preceded for twenty minutes by a shimmering zigzag in her right visual field, followed by a throbbing left sided headache with nausea and light sensitivity lasting most of a day. The visual disturbance resolves completely before the headache begins. She does not smoke, her blood pressure today is 112/70 mmHg, and her body mass index is 22. She has no personal or family history of venous thromboembolism or stroke, and she takes no regular medication.

data_table.Vital signs: Blood pressure 112/70 mmHg, pulse rate 68/min, other observations within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Body mass index 22, neurological examination normal between episodes, visual fields full to confrontation, fundoscopy normal
data_table.Investigations: None performed

lead_in: What contraception should you recommend?

options.text: A progestogen only method such as the implant, the intrauterine device or the pill
A low dose combined pill containing 20 micrograms of ethinylestradiol with monitoring
A combined pill taken continuously, since her headaches occur in the hormone free week
Copper intrauterine device only, because hormonal contraception is unsafe in migraine
A combined vaginal ring, since non oral delivery avoids the first pass hepatic effect

subtopic_detail: whether laparoscopy is needed before treating cyclical pelvic pain with a typical history
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 24-year-old woman with four years of pelvic pain that begins two days before each period, continues through the heaviest days, and has recently started to occur with deep penetration during intercourse. She misses one or two days of work most months.

Ibuprofen taken when the pain is already severe helps a little. She has never been pregnant, does not want to conceive for at least four years and currently uses condoms. There is no bleeding between periods, no bowel or bladder symptoms, and no fevers or weight loss. Her mother had a hysterectomy in her thirties for pelvic pain. Examination shows a mobile anteverted uterus with mild tenderness in the posterior fornix and no palpable mass or nodularity. Pelvic ultrasound reports normal ovaries with no endometrioma.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Anteverted mobile uterus, mild posterior fornix tenderness, no adnexal mass, no palpable nodularity, speculum examination normal
data_table.Investigations: Transvaginal ultrasound normal ovaries with no endometrioma, chlamydia nucleic acid test negative, full blood count normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first treatment?

options.text: A gonadotropin releasing hormone agonist with add back hormone therapy for six months
Refer to a pelvic pain physiotherapist and a psychologist as the initial management plan
Diagnostic laparoscopy with excision of any lesions before starting medical treatment
Magnetic resonance imaging of the pelvis to stage the disease before choosing treatment
Continuous combined hormonal contraception with a regular anti inflammatory before pain starts

subtopic_detail: explaining what a high chance result on a maternal plasma screening test does and does not establish
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 39-year-old woman at 10 weeks in her third pregnancy who asks for the blood test that checks the baby's chromosomes. She says a friend had it and was told everything was fine, and she wants to avoid the needle in the abdomen that her sister had.

She has two healthy children born at term, no family history of chromosomal or genetic conditions, and no consanguinity. She takes folic acid and no other medication. Her dating scan yesterday showed a single viable intrauterine pregnancy at 10 weeks and 1 day with a normal appearance. She has private health insurance and asks whether the test is covered by Medicare.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Uterus not palpable abdominally, no abnormality on general examination
data_table.Investigations: Dating ultrasound single viable intrauterine pregnancy at 10 weeks and 1 day, booking bloods unremarkable

lead_in: What is the most important point to cover when counselling her?

options.text: Her age of 39 makes the test mandatory before any further antenatal care proceeds
A low chance result excludes chromosomal and genetic conditions in this pregnancy
The test replaces the need for the nuchal translucency and morphology ultrasounds
A high chance result estimates risk and needs a diagnostic test to confirm it
The test is rebated through Medicare for all women aged 35 years and over

subtopic_detail: Timing of birth for intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy when the bile acid level exceeds one hundred micromol per litre
stem:
A 31-year-old woman at 33 weeks in her first pregnancy attends your antenatal clinic with three weeks of itching, worst on her palms and the soles of her feet and worse at night. She has no rash apart from scratch marks.

Her pregnancy has otherwise been uncomplicated with normal growth on serial scans and normal blood pressure throughout. Her urine shows no protein. A viral hepatitis screen and liver autoantibodies are negative, and a liver ultrasound shows no biliary dilatation or gallstones. Her fasting bile acid level today is 128 micromol/L, having been 46 micromol/L two weeks ago.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 84/min, blood pressure 112/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7 °C, fetal heart rate 142/min
data_table.Investigations: Bile acids 128 micromol/L (<10), alanine aminotransferase 96 U/L (<35), bilirubin 12 micromol/L (<20), platelets 245 x10^9/L (150-400)
data_table.Imaging: Liver ultrasound shows no biliary dilatation and no gallstones, fetal growth on the 45th centile

lead_in: What is the most appropriate plan for timing of birth?

options.text: Plan birth at 35 to 36 weeks after a course of antenatal corticosteroids
Plan birth at 38 to 39 weeks with weekly bile acid monitoring until then
Plan birth at 37 weeks with twice weekly cardiotocography until then
Plan birth at 40 weeks and treat the itch with ursodeoxycholic acid until then
Arrange birth within the next 24 hours by induction regardless of cervical status

subtopic_detail: Anti-D requirement for a woman with a rhesus negative blood group and light bleeding at ten weeks with a closed cervix
stem:
A 27-year-old woman in her second pregnancy attends your early pregnancy assessment unit at 10 weeks with two days of light vaginal bleeding, described as spotting that does not fill a pad. She has mild period like cramping that settles with paracetamol.

Her first pregnancy ended in a normal vaginal birth three years ago and she received anti-D immunoglobulin after that birth. Speculum examination shows a closed cervical os with a small amount of old blood in the vagina, and no products are visible. Ultrasound today confirms a single intrauterine pregnancy with a fetal heart rate of 164/min and a crown rump length consistent with dates. Her blood group is confirmed as O negative and her antibody screen is negative.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Closed cervical os, small amount of old blood in the vagina, no products of conception visible, uterus non-tender
data_table.Investigations: Blood group O negative, antibody screen negative, haemoglobin 128 g/L (115-155)
data_table.Imaging: Single intrauterine pregnancy, fetal heart rate 164/min, crown rump length consistent with 10 weeks

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management of her rhesus status?

options.text: Give 250 IU of anti-D immunoglobulin now and repeat the dose if bleeding continues
Withhold anti-D immunoglobulin and manage expectantly with review if bleeding worsens
Give 625 IU of anti-D immunoglobulin now and arrange a Kleihauer test the same day
Arrange non-invasive fetal rhesus genotyping now and give anti-D only if the result is positive
Withhold anti-D immunoglobulin now and omit the routine third trimester doses as well

subtopic_detail: Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes at thirty weeks with no clinical infection and a cephalic presentation
stem:
A 29-year-old woman at 30 weeks in her second pregnancy presents to your birth suite after a sudden gush of clear fluid four hours ago, with continued leaking since. She has no abdominal pain and reports normal fetal movements.

Sterile speculum examination shows a pool of clear liquor in the posterior fornix with a closed cervix and no offensive odour. Her uterus is soft and non-tender on palpation, and the presentation is cephalic on ultrasound with an amniotic fluid index at the lower limit of normal. Cardiotocography shows a baseline of 140/min with normal variability, accelerations present and no decelerations. Her observations and blood results are reassuring.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 82/min, blood pressure 114/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.8 °C, fetal heart rate baseline 140/min
data_table.Examination: Pool of clear liquor in the posterior fornix, closed cervix, no offensive odour, soft non-tender uterus
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 9.8 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), C-reactive protein 4 mg/L (<5), low vaginal swab sent

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Oral amoxicillin with clavulanate and corticosteroids with inpatient expectant surveillance
Oral erythromycin with antenatal corticosteroids and inpatient expectant surveillance
Antenatal corticosteroids with tocolysis for 48 hours and inpatient expectant surveillance
Antenatal corticosteroids with induction of labour once the second dose has been given
Antenatal corticosteroids with amnioinfusion and inpatient expectant surveillance

subtopic_detail: Antenatal surveillance and birth planning after a low anterior placenta is reported in a woman with two previous caesareans
stem:
A 34-year-old woman at 21 weeks in her third pregnancy attends your antenatal clinic to discuss her morphology scan. Her two previous births were both by caesarean section, the first for breech presentation and the second as a planned repeat procedure.

She is well with no bleeding and no pain. The morphology scan reports an anterior placenta that reaches the internal os, with loss of the normal hypoechoic retroplacental clear zone and several irregular vascular lacunae within the placental substance in the region overlying the previous uterine scar. Fetal growth and anatomy are normal. She tells you she has read that a low placenta usually moves up, and asks whether she can plan to give birth at her local unit as she did last time.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Imaging: Anterior placenta reaching the internal os, loss of the retroplacental clear zone, irregular vascular lacunae overlying the previous uterine scar, normal fetal growth and anatomy
data_table.Obstetric history: Two previous caesarean sections, no antepartum bleeding in this pregnancy

lead_in: What is the most appropriate plan?

options.text: Refer to a tertiary centre for specialist imaging and a planned caesarean with surgical backup
Repeat the transvaginal scan at 32 weeks and plan a caesarean locally if it remains low
Reassure her that most low placentas resolve and review the position again at 36 weeks
Admit her from 28 weeks for inpatient observation with a planned caesarean at her local unit
Arrange magnetic resonance imaging now and plan a caesarean hysterectomy at 34 weeks locally

subtopic_detail: Loss of the presenting part and a fetal bradycardia during labour in a woman with one previous caesarean
stem:
You are called to review a 32-year-old woman at 39 weeks labouring spontaneously after one previous caesarean section for failure to progress. She has been progressing well and was 7 cm dilated with the head at the level of the spines thirty minutes ago.

Her epidural has been working well, but over the last few minutes she has become distressed by constant lower abdominal pain that persists between contractions, which is new. The cardiotocograph now shows a prolonged deceleration to 70/min lasting four minutes with no recovery. On vaginal examination the presenting part is now high and difficult to reach. Her contractions, which had been regular, have become infrequent and weak, and there is light fresh vaginal bleeding.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 126/min, blood pressure 96/54 mmHg, respiratory rate 24/min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.9 °C, fetal heart rate 70/min
data_table.Examination: Constant lower abdominal pain between contractions, presenting part high and difficult to reach, light fresh vaginal bleeding, contractions infrequent and weak
data_table.Monitoring: Prolonged deceleration to 70/min for four minutes with no recovery

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.text: Give a subcutaneous tocolytic and reassess the fetal heart rate over the next ten minutes
Perform an amniotomy and apply a fetal scalp electrode to improve the quality of the trace
Reposition her into the left lateral position and give a fluid bolus with high flow oxygen
Commence an oxytocin infusion to restore contractions and reassess progress in thirty minutes
Call the theatre team for immediate laparotomy with the neonatal and anaesthetic teams

subtopic_detail: Maternal collapse with a mass visible at the introitus immediately after the placenta is delivered
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar called to a 24-year-old woman who has just given birth to her first baby. The placenta was delivered a few minutes ago and she immediately became pale and clammy with severe lower abdominal pain, and her blood pressure has fallen sharply.

Estimated blood loss so far is about 500 mL, which does not account for the degree of shock. On examination you cannot feel the uterine fundus abdominally where you would expect it. A dark red mass is visible at the introitus with the placenta already separated from it. Her midwife tells you she gave the routine oxytocin with the birth of the anterior shoulder and applied cord traction as the placenta delivered.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 58/min, blood pressure 74/38 mmHg, respiratory rate 24/min, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 36.5 °C
data_table.Examination: Uterine fundus not palpable abdominally, dark red mass visible at the introitus with the placenta separated, pale and clammy
data_table.Blood loss: Estimated 500 mL, disproportionate to the degree of shock

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.text: Replace the fundus manually at once while further uterotonic drugs are withheld
Give a bolus of intravenous oxytocin at once and then attempt to replace the fundus
Insert an intrauterine balloon tamponade device and inflate it to control the bleeding
Apply bimanual uterine compression and commence a rapid crystalloid fluid infusion
Transfer immediately to theatre for laparotomy and surgical correction of the abnormality

subtopic_detail: Failure to establish breastfeeding with lethargy and low sodium in a woman who had a large blood loss at birth
stem:
A 29-year-old woman is reviewed on your postnatal ward on day nine after a birth complicated by a 2.8 litre haemorrhage requiring transfusion of six units of red cells and a period of hypotension in theatre.

She has been readmitted with four days of increasing tiredness, dizziness on standing and poor appetite. She has produced almost no breast milk despite regular expressing and good support from the lactation consultant, and she has noticed she feels cold all the time. Her lochia is normal and her uterus is well involuted and non-tender. Her haemoglobin has been stable since discharge and her iron studies are satisfactory after the transfusion.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 92/min, blood pressure 88/54 mmHg lying with a fall on standing, respiratory rate 18/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.1 °C
data_table.Examination: Uterus well involuted and non-tender, normal lochia, no calf tenderness, minimal breast fullness despite regular expressing
data_table.Investigations: Sodium 126 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 4.4 mmol/L (3.5-5.5), glucose 3.1 mmol/L (3.5-7.8), haemoglobin 104 g/L (115-155), thyroid stimulating hormone 0.4 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), free thyroxine 7 pmol/L (9-19)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial treatment?

options.text: Oral thyroxine replacement started now with hydrocortisone added once the results return
Fluid restriction to 1 litre daily with paired serum and urine osmolality measurements
Intravenous hydrocortisone given before any thyroid hormone replacement is started
Domperidone to stimulate lactation with dietitian review and iron supplementation
Hypertonic saline infusion to correct the sodium with close neurological observation

subtopic_detail: Anticoagulation planning before conception for a woman with a mechanical mitral valve prosthesis
stem:
A 30-year-old woman attends your general practice to discuss trying for a pregnancy. She had a mechanical mitral valve replacement four years ago for rheumatic valve disease and takes warfarin 4 mg daily, with a target international normalised ratio of 3.0 and consistently stable readings.

She is otherwise well with good exercise tolerance and no breathlessness or palpitations. She has read online that warfarin harms the baby and tells you she has already decided to stop it as soon as her pregnancy test is positive. She has not yet stopped contraception. Her most recent echocardiogram showed a normally functioning prosthesis with good ventricular function.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Mechanical first heart sound audible, no murmur of prosthetic dysfunction, no peripheral oedema, good exercise tolerance
data_table.Investigations: International normalised ratio 3.0 and stable on warfarin 4 mg daily, echocardiogram shows normally functioning prosthesis with good ventricular function

lead_in: What is the most appropriate advice?

options.text: Refer now for a joint cardiac and obstetric plan before she stops any anticoagulant
Agree with her plan to stop warfarin as soon as a pregnancy test is positive
Advise her to switch to a direct oral anticoagulant before she stops contraception
Advise her to switch to aspirin with clopidogrel before she stops contraception
Reassure her that warfarin is safe throughout pregnancy and no change will be needed

subtopic_detail: Absent periods at sixteen with short stature and minimal breast development in a girl whose pubic hair is normal
stem:
A 16-year-old girl attends your practice with her mother because she has never had a period. Her mother reached menarche at 13 and her older sister at 12.

She has always been the shortest in her class and her height today is well below the third centile, against a mid-parental target on the 50th. Breast development is minimal, while pubic and axillary hair are normal for her age. She has no headaches, no visual symptoms and a normal sense of smell, and she is not underweight and does not exercise excessively. On examination she has a broad chest with widely spaced nipples and there is a soft mid-systolic murmur at the left sternal edge. Her pregnancy test is negative.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 74/min, blood pressure 128/82 mmHg in the right arm, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 °C
data_table.Examination: Height well below the third centile, breast stage 2, normal pubic and axillary hair, broad chest with widely spaced nipples, soft mid-systolic murmur at the left sternal edge
data_table.Investigations: Pregnancy test negative, thyroid function and prolactin within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Start combined oral contraceptive therapy now to induce withdrawal bleeding and breast development
Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the pituitary before any other investigation is undertaken
Reassure her that this represents constitutional delay and review her again in twelve months
Measure gonadotrophins and arrange a karyotype before any hormone treatment is started
Measure total testosterone and arrange a pelvic ultrasound to assess for androgen excess

subtopic_detail: Investigation offered to a couple after a third consecutive first trimester loss with no living children
stem:
A 31-year-old woman attends your practice with her partner two weeks after a third consecutive miscarriage, all at between seven and nine weeks. They have no living children and she conceives readily each time.

Her cycles are regular at 29 days and she has no history of pelvic infection, uterine surgery or termination. She is a non-smoker with a body mass index of 24 kg/m2 and takes no regular medication. Her thyroid function and a random glucose are normal, and her cervical screening is up to date. The couple are distressed and want to know what can be looked for before they try again.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Unremarkable abdominal and pelvic examination, no adnexal mass or tenderness
data_table.Investigations: Thyroid function within normal limits, random glucose 4.9 mmol/L (3.5-7.8), full blood count within normal limits

lead_in: What investigations would you arrange?

options.text: Test for inherited thrombophilias and image the uterine cavity, with parental karyotyping discussed
Test for natural killer cell activity and image the uterine cavity, with parental karyotyping discussed
Test for antiphospholipid antibodies and image the uterine cavity, with parental karyotyping discussed
Test sperm DNA fragmentation and image the uterine cavity, with parental karyotyping discussed
Arrange no investigations at this stage and advise trying again with reassurance about the prognosis

subtopic_detail: Magnesium sulfate for neuroprotection in established very preterm labour in a normotensive woman
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar on the birth suite reviewing a woman at 28 weeks and 3 days in her second pregnancy. She was admitted six hours ago with regular painful contractions and her membranes ruptured spontaneously thirty minutes ago.

Her cervix is now 5 cm dilated and the midwife expects birth within a few hours. She completed a course of betamethasone yesterday after her first assessment. Her blood pressure has been normal throughout the pregnancy, her reflexes are normal and her urine shows no protein. The neonatal team has been called to attend.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 92/min, blood pressure 118/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.9 °C, fetal heart rate 148/min
data_table.Examination: Cervix 5 cm dilated, cephalic presentation, clear liquor draining
data_table.Investigations: Urinalysis shows no protein, full blood count and renal function within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate addition to her management?

options.text: Withhold magnesium because her blood pressure and reflexes are normal
Give magnesium sulfate only if she develops signs of pre-eclampsia
Give nifedipine alone to delay birth and omit magnesium altogether
Give magnesium sulfate now for fetal neuroprotection before birth
Defer magnesium until after birth and give it to the baby directly

subtopic_detail: Definitive drainage technique for a recurrent vulval gland abscess after repeated simple incision
stem:
A 32-year-old woman presents to your practice with a painful swelling at the entrance to the vagina that has grown over three days and now makes sitting and walking uncomfortable.

This is her third such episode in eighteen months. On each of the two previous occasions she attended an emergency department, where the swelling was cut and drained under local anaesthetic, and each time it returned within a few months. On examination there is a tender fluctuant swelling about 4 cm across in the posterior part of the vulva on the right, with surrounding erythema but no spreading cellulitis. She is systemically well and has no other symptoms.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Tender fluctuant 4 cm swelling in the right posterior vulva, overlying erythema, no induration of surrounding tissue
data_table.Past history: Two previous episodes each treated by simple incision and drainage, both recurring within months

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management of this episode?

options.text: Simple incision and drainage under local anaesthetic in the department
Oral antibiotics alone with warm compresses and review in one week
Complete surgical excision of the gland under general anaesthetic
Needle aspiration of the swelling with a wide bore needle in clinic
Insertion of a Word catheter to create a permanently draining tract

subtopic_detail: Sequencing thiamine before glucose containing fluid in prolonged vomiting of early pregnancy
stem:
You are the medical officer admitting a woman at 11 weeks in her first pregnancy who has been vomiting many times a day for four weeks and can no longer keep down fluids.

She has lost 6 kg since her booking weight and looks dry, with reduced skin turgor and dry mucous membranes. Her urine shows heavy ketones. The resident has already written up an initial litre of five per cent dextrose and an antiemetic, and asks you to check the chart before it is hung. She has taken no supplements since the vomiting began and her only other history is mild asthma.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 112/min, blood pressure 96/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.5 °C
data_table.Examination: Dry mucous membranes, reduced skin turgor, no abdominal tenderness, no goitre
data_table.Investigations: Urinalysis shows heavy ketones, potassium 3.2 mmol/L (3.5-5.5), sodium 133 mmol/L (135-145), thyroid function within normal limits
data_table.Weight: Loss of 6 kg from a booking weight of 68 kg

lead_in: What change to the prescribed fluid plan is most important?

options.text: Start five per cent dextrose and add an antiemetic once she settles
Start normal saline and give oral thiamine tablets once she can swallow
Give parenteral thiamine before starting any glucose containing fluid
Start potassium replacement first and withhold thiamine until admission
Start total parenteral nutrition given the degree of weight she has lost

subtopic_detail: Preventive therapy for culture proven recurrent urinary infection after menopause with a normal tract
stem:
A 68-year-old woman attends your practice frustrated by repeated urinary infections. She has had four culture proven episodes in the past twelve months, each with dysuria and frequency, and each settling promptly with a short course of antibiotics.

She went through menopause at 51 and has never used hormone therapy. She describes vaginal dryness and discomfort with intercourse. On examination the vulval and vaginal tissues are pale and thin with loss of rugae, and there is no prolapse beyond the hymen. A bladder scan after voiding shows a negligible residual volume, and an ultrasound of the renal tract arranged by a colleague was reported as normal.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Pale thin vaginal epithelium with loss of rugae, no prolapse beyond the hymen, no suprapubic tenderness
data_table.Investigations: Four culture proven infections in twelve months with fully sensitive Escherichia coli, post-void residual negligible, renal tract ultrasound reported as normal
data_table.Glucose: Fasting glucose and HbA1c within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate preventive treatment?

options.text: Long term low dose trimethoprim taken each night for the next six months
A further course of antibiotics given at the onset of each new episode
Cranberry capsules taken daily together with an increased fluid intake
Topical vaginal oestrogen used regularly as ongoing preventive therapy
Referral for cystoscopy to exclude a structural cause for the infections

subtopic_detail: Timing of combined hormonal contraception for a breastfeeding woman in the first week after birth
stem:
You are reviewing a 30-year-old woman on the postnatal ward on day 5 after an uncomplicated vaginal birth of her second child. She is fully breastfeeding and the baby is feeding well.

She used a combined oral contraceptive pill before this pregnancy, got on well with it, and asks to restart the same brand before she goes home today so that nothing is forgotten. She has no personal or family history of venous thromboembolism, does not smoke, and her blood pressure and body mass index are both normal. Her first child was conceived sooner than she had planned and she is anxious to avoid that happening again.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Uterus well contracted, lochia normal, calves soft and non-tender
data_table.History: Fully breastfeeding, no thrombotic history, non smoker, body mass index 23 kg/m2
data_table.Birth details: Uncomplicated vaginal birth at term, estimated blood loss 300 mL

lead_in: What is the most appropriate advice about her contraceptive request?

options.text: Defer combined hormonal contraception until six weeks after the birth
Start combined hormonal contraception today before she goes home
Start combined hormonal contraception at three weeks after the birth
Advise that breastfeeding alone gives reliable contraception for a year
Defer all hormonal contraception until she has stopped breastfeeding

subtopic_detail: Stratifying a complex adnexal mass in a postmenopausal woman to decide the surgical pathway
stem:
A 62-year-old woman attends your practice with three months of abdominal bloating, feeling full after small meals and a vague dragging discomfort in the pelvis. She has lost 4 kg without trying.

She went through menopause at 50 and has had no bleeding since. Her abdomen is distended with shifting dullness, and bimanual examination reveals a firm irregular mass arising from the pelvis. She has no family history of breast or ovarian cancer. Her bowel habit is unchanged and a faecal occult blood test arranged by a colleague was negative. The imaging and tumour marker you requested have now returned.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Distended abdomen with shifting dullness, firm irregular pelvic mass, no lymphadenopathy
data_table.Ultrasound: 9 cm multilocular right adnexal mass with solid areas and internal vascularity, moderate ascites, normal endometrial thickness

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her management?

options.text: Arrange laparoscopic ovarian cystectomy at the local hospital next month
Repeat the ultrasound and tumour marker in three months to see if they change
Arrange image guided percutaneous biopsy of the mass before any referral
Refer to the general gynaecology list for laparoscopic oophorectomy locally
Calculate the risk of malignancy index and refer to gynaecological oncology

subtopic_detail: Choosing intrapartum prophylaxis when the recorded penicillin reaction is a delayed childhood rash
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar asked to write up intrapartum antibiotics for a woman at 39 weeks who is 4 cm dilated with intact membranes. Her screening swab at 36 weeks grew group B streptococcus.

Her notes carry an allergy label for penicillin. When you ask her about it directly, she describes a flat blotchy rash over her tummy and back that appeared three or four days into a course of amoxicillin for a sore throat when she was about six years old. It settled over a week without treatment. She has never had swelling of the lips or tongue, wheeze, faintness or blistering, and she has taken cefalexin for a urinary infection since then without trouble.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 88/min, blood pressure 122/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.8 °C, fetal heart rate 140/min
data_table.Screening: Vaginal and rectal swab at 36 weeks positive for group B streptococcus, susceptibility not requested
data_table.Allergy history: Delayed maculopapular rash on day three or four of amoxicillin at age six, no mucosal or respiratory involvement, subsequent cefalexin tolerated
data_table.Labour: Cervix 4 cm dilated, membranes intact, contracting three in ten minutes

lead_in: Which intrapartum antibiotic is most appropriate?

options.text: Intravenous benzylpenicillin despite the allergy recorded in her notes
Intravenous vancomycin because she reports an allergy to penicillin
Intravenous cefazolin because her reported reaction was not severe
Intravenous clindamycin without testing the isolate for susceptibility
Oral amoxicillin once labour is established and repeated six hourly

subtopic_detail: Deciding on a repeat antenatal corticosteroid course four weeks after the first when birth again appears likely
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar reviewing a woman at 30 weeks and 2 days who has been readmitted with regular painful contractions and a cervix that has shortened on transvaginal scan since her last assessment.

She was admitted four weeks ago with threatened preterm labour, received a complete course of betamethasone then, and settled without giving birth. On that occasion the contractions stopped within a day. This time her contractions are stronger and more frequent, her cervical length has fallen considerably and the consultant judges that birth within the next week is likely. Her membranes are intact, her observations are normal and there is no evidence of infection.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 90/min, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 17/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.9 °C, fetal heart rate 144/min
data_table.Previous treatment: Complete betamethasone course given four weeks ago at 26 weeks and 2 days
data_table.Current findings: Cervical length 12 mm on transvaginal ultrasound, contracting three in ten minutes, membranes intact
data_table.Investigations: White cell count and C reactive protein within normal limits, glucose within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate decision regarding corticosteroids?

options.text: Give a full new two dose course every week until she gives birth
Withhold repeat steroids because a course has already been given
Withhold repeat steroids because she is now beyond 30 weeks gestation
Give a repeat course only once the membranes have actually ruptured
Give a single repeat course as birth is likely within the next week

subtopic_detail: Management of a positive routine antenatal urine culture in a woman without urinary symptoms
stem:
A 26-year-old woman at 16 weeks in her first pregnancy attends your practice to discuss the results of her booking investigations. She feels well and is getting on with the pregnancy without difficulty.

She has no urinary frequency, dysuria, urgency, haematuria or loin pain, and she has had no fevers. The midstream specimen collected at her booking visit has grown a significant pure growth of Escherichia coli, fully sensitive on the panel reported. Her renal function is within normal limits and she has no history of urinary tract infection or renal tract abnormality.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft and non-tender, no renal angle tenderness
data_table.Microbiology: Midstream urine culture with a significant pure growth of Escherichia coli, fully sensitive
data_table.Other results: Renal function within normal limits, no proteinuria, full blood count within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Treat with an oral antibiotic guided by susceptibility and repeat the culture
Repeat the urine culture and treat only if symptoms develop later
No treatment as bacteriuria without symptoms needs no antibiotic
Treat only if a repeat culture also grows the same organism in a week
Refer for renal tract ultrasound before considering any antibiotic

subtopic_detail: Initial ward management of a first bleed at 32 weeks when the placenta covers the internal os
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar called to the assessment unit to see a 34-year-old woman in her third pregnancy at 32 weeks. She was sitting watching television when she felt a sudden gush and found bright red blood soaking her clothing.

She has had no abdominal pain at any point and felt no contractions. The bleeding amounted to roughly 200 mL and has now settled to light spotting. Her uterus is soft and completely non-tender on palpation, and the baby has been moving normally. Her morphology scan reported a low placenta and a repeat transvaginal scan a fortnight ago confirmed that it covers the internal os. Her blood group is O positive and her haemoglobin is within normal limits.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 92/min, blood pressure 116/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7 °C, fetal heart rate 142/min
data_table.Examination: Soft non-tender uterus, cephalic presentation high, light fresh spotting on the pad, no contractions palpable
data_table.Imaging: Transvaginal ultrasound a fortnight ago shows the placenta covering the internal os
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin within normal limits, blood group O positive, coagulation profile within normal limits, group and hold sent
data_table.Cardiotocograph: Baseline 142/min with normal variability and no decelerations

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Perform a digital vaginal examination to assess the cervix for dilatation
Admit for observation and corticosteroids, avoiding digital vaginal examination
Discharge home with advice to return if the bleeding recurs or worsens
Proceed to immediate caesarean section regardless of the bleeding settling
Induce labour with prostaglandin now that the bleeding has settled down

subtopic_detail: Continuing and monitoring an anticonvulsant whose clearance rises sharply through pregnancy
stem:
A 29-year-old woman attends your clinic at 7 weeks in a pregnancy she is pleased about but had not planned. She has focal epilepsy and has been free of seizures for three years on lamotrigine monotherapy.

She drives to work and cares for a toddler. Having read about medication in pregnancy overnight, she tells you she has already missed this morning's dose and intends to stop the tablets altogether until the baby is born. She has no other medical history, takes no other medication and had not been taking folic acid before conception. Her last seizure was a focal to bilateral tonic clonic event.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Epilepsy history: Focal epilepsy, seizure free for three years on lamotrigine monotherapy, last event was focal to bilateral tonic clonic
data_table.Medication: Lamotrigine monotherapy, no other medication, no preconception folic acid
data_table.Social: Holds a current driver licence, sole daytime carer for a toddler

lead_in: What is the most appropriate advice?

options.text: Continue the lamotrigine and monitor drug levels through each trimester
Stop the lamotrigine now because it is unsafe in the first trimester
Switch to sodium valproate which is better studied during pregnancy
Halve the lamotrigine dose to reduce fetal exposure during organogenesis
Continue the current dose without any monitoring of drug levels

subtopic_detail: Antithyroid drug selection by trimester in a woman with Graves disease who has just conceived
stem:
A 27-year-old woman telephones your clinic to say her pregnancy test is positive. Her last menstrual period was six weeks ago and the pregnancy was planned.

She has Graves disease diagnosed two years ago and has been stable on carbimazole for the past nine months, with thyroid function in the target range at her last two checks and no goitre symptoms. She has no palpitations, tremor or weight loss at present. She asks whether she should keep taking her tablets now that she is pregnant, and mentions that she stopped her regular blood tests a few months ago because everything had been stable.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Small smooth goitre, no tremor, no lid lag, no proptosis
data_table.Thyroid function: Free thyroxine and thyroid stimulating hormone within the target range on the two most recent checks
data_table.Medication: Carbimazole at a stable dose for nine months

lead_in: What is the most appropriate change to her treatment?

options.text: Stop all antithyroid medication and monitor thyroid function monthly
Change to propylthiouracil for the first trimester and then review
Continue carbimazole at the same dose throughout the whole pregnancy
Add levothyroxine alongside carbimazole to block and replace instead
Refer for thyroidectomy in the first trimester to avoid drug exposure

subtopic_detail: Severe localised pain over a known fibroid in the second trimester with a closed cervix
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar reviewing a 33-year-old woman at 22 weeks in her first pregnancy who presented overnight with severe constant pain in the left side of her abdomen that began two days ago and has steadily worsened.

She has a fibroid uterus documented at her morphology scan, with the largest measuring 8 cm on the left side of the fundus. The pain is sharply localised and she can point to it with one finger. Her uterus is soft between examinations and is tender only directly over the fibroid, with no generalised tenderness. Her cervix is long and closed on speculum examination and there is no bleeding or fluid loss. Her urine culture is negative and her cardiotocograph is reassuring.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 96/min, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 37.6 °C, fetal heart rate 148/min
data_table.Examination: Tenderness localised over the left fundal fibroid only, uterus soft elsewhere, cervix long and closed, no bleeding
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 13.2 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), C reactive protein 32 mg/L (less than 5), urine culture negative
data_table.Imaging: Ultrasound shows an 8 cm left fundal fibroid with heterogeneous echotexture, normal liquor volume, normal fetal growth

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Urgent laparotomy and myomectomy to remove the painful fibroid
Start intravenous antibiotics for presumed intrauterine infection
Analgesia and observation without any operative intervention
Uterine artery embolisation to infarct the fibroid and relieve pain
Induce labour because the pain indicates the pregnancy cannot continue

subtopic_detail: Preconception planning for a woman established on an antiepileptic drug
stem:
A 28-year-old woman attends your general practice to discuss trying for a baby in the next few months. She has focal epilepsy and has been seizure free for three years on lamotrigine 200 mg twice daily.

She takes no other regular medication, has no history of neural tube defect in her family and her body mass index is 24 kg/m2. She has read online that epilepsy medication causes birth defects and has already stopped taking her tablets for the last four days. She has not yet conceived and her last menstrual period was ten days ago.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Neurological examination normal, no focal deficit
data_table.Medication: Lamotrigine 200 mg twice daily, self ceased four days ago, no other regular medication
data_table.History: Focal epilepsy, seizure free for three years, no family history of neural tube defect, body mass index 24 kg/m2

lead_in: What would you first recommend?

options.text: Support stopping lamotrigine and begin folic acid 5 mg daily
Switch her to sodium valproate and begin folic acid 5 mg daily
Restart lamotrigine now and begin folic acid 0.5 mg daily
Restart lamotrigine now and begin folic acid 5 mg daily
Defer any change until she has a positive pregnancy test

subtopic_detail: Timing of pertussis containing vaccine within the current pregnancy
stem:
A 30-year-old woman attends your antenatal clinic at 22 weeks in her second pregnancy. She asks about whooping cough because a colleague's baby was admitted to hospital with it last month.

She received a pertussis containing vaccine during her first pregnancy three years ago and tells you she assumed that would still cover this baby. She has had an influenza vaccine this season. She has no allergy to vaccine components, no immunosuppression and has had no adverse reaction to previous vaccination. The pregnancy is uncomplicated with normal growth on ultrasound. She plans to breastfeed.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 80 beats per minute, blood pressure 110/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius, fetal heart rate 145 beats per minute
data_table.Examination: Symphysis fundal height 22 cm, no abnormality detected
data_table.Immunisation history: Pertussis containing vaccine in a previous pregnancy three years ago, influenza vaccine this season, no vaccine allergy
data_table.Pregnancy: Uncomplicated, normal growth on ultrasound, 22 weeks gestation

lead_in: What is the most appropriate advice about pertussis vaccination?

options.text: Explain that her previous dose protects this baby as well
Defer the vaccine until she has given birth to this baby
Defer the vaccine until she reaches thirty six weeks gestation
Vaccinate the household contacts instead of vaccinating her
Give the vaccine now between twenty and thirty two weeks

subtopic_detail: Determining chorionicity in a newly confirmed twin pregnancy
stem:
A 27-year-old woman attends your general practice at 8 weeks in her first pregnancy. A dating ultrasound arranged after a positive test has reported two gestational sacs with two live embryos of equal size.

The report does not comment on the membrane or on the number of placentas. She is well, has no bleeding and no pain, and has already started folic acid and iodine supplementation. She has no family history of twins and conceived spontaneously. She asks whether the twins are identical and what this means for her care. Her body mass index is 23 kg/m2 and her booking bloods are unremarkable.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Abdominal and pelvic examination unremarkable
data_table.Ultrasound: Two gestational sacs each containing a live embryo of equal crown rump length, membrane characteristics and placental number not reported
data_table.History: Spontaneous conception, first pregnancy, folic acid and iodine already commenced

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Arrange ultrasound between eleven and thirteen weeks to assess the membrane
Arrange non-invasive prenatal testing to determine whether they are identical
Arrange a repeat ultrasound at twenty weeks with the morphology scan
Reassure her that two separate sacs means the twins are not identical
Refer her directly for fortnightly scans from sixteen weeks onwards

subtopic_detail: Rubella non immune status identified on booking bloods and acted on after birth
stem:
You are the resident doing the postnatal round on day one. A 26-year-old woman gave birth yesterday to a healthy term boy and is establishing breastfeeding well.

Her booking bloods, which you are reviewing before discharge, show that she is rubella non immune. She was born overseas and has no record of childhood immunisation. Her blood group is O rhesus D positive, her full blood count is normal and she had no antenatal complications. She tells you she and her partner would like another baby fairly soon and asks whether anything needs doing before they start trying.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Uterus well contracted, lochia normal, perineum intact, breastfeeding established
data_table.Investigations: Rubella immunoglobulin G non immune on booking bloods, blood group O rhesus D positive, full blood count within normal limits, hepatitis B surface antigen negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Give rubella immunoglobulin before she goes home tomorrow
Give measles mumps rubella vaccine before she goes home
Arrange vaccination once she has finished breastfeeding him
Repeat her rubella serology in six weeks before deciding
Vaccinate her partner and the baby to protect her instead

subtopic_detail: Primary amenorrhoea with short stature and absent breast development
stem:
A 16-year-old girl attends your general practice with her mother because she has never had a period. Her mother says she has always been the shortest in her year and that she has not grown noticeably since she was about 13.

She has no headaches, no visual symptoms and a normal sense of smell. She is not underweight, does not exercise excessively and has no features of androgen excess. She has no cyclical pelvic pain. Examination shows Tanner stage 1 breast development with sparse pubic hair, a high arched palate, a wide chest with widely spaced nipples and a low posterior hairline. Blood pressure is equal in both arms and femoral pulses are palpable.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 76 beats per minute, blood pressure 118/74 mmHg in both arms, respiratory rate 15 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Height 142 cm well below the 3rd centile, body mass index 22 kg/m2, Tanner stage 1 breast development, sparse pubic hair, high arched palate, wide carrying angle, low posterior hairline, femoral pulses present
data_table.Investigations: Follicle stimulating hormone 62 IU/L (3-10 follicular), luteinising hormone 28 IU/L, oestradiol less than 50 pmol/L, prolactin and thyroid function within normal limits, pregnancy test negative
data_table.Imaging: Pelvic ultrasound shows a small uterus with streak ovaries

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Request pituitary imaging studies
Measure her serum testosterone
Request a peripheral blood karyotype
Arrange a progestogen challenge
Arrange coeliac disease serology

subtopic_detail: Rapidly progressive fever and hypotension on day two after a vaginal birth
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar called to the postnatal ward at 2 am. A 30-year-old woman who gave birth vaginally 36 hours ago has become rapidly unwell over the past three hours with rigors and severe lower abdominal pain.

Her midwife reports the lochia has an offensive smell. Her 4-year-old was sent home from childcare last week with a sore throat. The perineum is intact with no tear and no haematoma, the calves are soft and non-tender, and there is no cough, no dysuria and no breast erythema. She is drowsy but rousable and her capillary refill is 4 seconds.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 138 beats per minute, blood pressure 82/44 mmHg, respiratory rate 32 breaths per minute, SpO2 95 percent on room air, temperature 39.4 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Drowsy but rousable, capillary refill 4 seconds, marked uterine tenderness with a bulky uterus, offensive lochia, perineum intact, calves soft, chest clear
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 2.1 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), C reactive protein 280 mg/L (less than 5), lactate 4.8 mmol/L (less than 2), creatinine 148 micromol/L (45-90), platelets 88 x10^9/L (150-400)
data_table.Social history: Household contact with a child who had a sore throat in the past week

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate antimicrobial management?

options.text: Give intravenous cefazolin with metronidazole now
Give oral amoxicillin with clavulanate and observe closely
Await blood culture results before starting any antibiotic
Give intravenous benzylpenicillin with clindamycin now
Give intravenous gentamicin alone and arrange urgent imaging

subtopic_detail: Counselling about mode of birth after a repaired third degree perineal tear
stem:
A 32-year-old woman attends your clinic to plan her second pregnancy. Two years ago she had a forceps birth complicated by a third degree perineal tear, which was repaired in theatre by a consultant at the time.

She tells you that she still cannot always hold wind, and that about once a fortnight she has to rush to the toilet and has twice not made it in time. She completed a course of pelvic floor physiotherapy after the birth with some improvement that then plateaued. Endoanal ultrasound arranged by the perineal clinic shows a persistent external anal sphincter defect and anorectal manometry shows a reduced squeeze pressure.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Well healed perineal scar, reduced voluntary anal squeeze on digital examination, no prolapse
data_table.Investigations: Endoanal ultrasound shows a persistent external anal sphincter defect, anorectal manometry shows reduced squeeze pressure, resting pressure preserved
data_table.Symptoms: Flatus incontinence most days and two episodes of faecal urgency incontinence in the past six months
data_table.Obstetric history: One forceps birth with a repaired third degree tear, no other deliveries

lead_in: What would you first recommend for her next birth?

options.text: Plan a vaginal birth with an elective mediolateral episiotomy
Plan a vaginal birth and repeat the physiotherapy beforehand
Plan a vaginal birth but avoid any instrumental assistance
Refer for secondary sphincter repair then plan a vaginal birth
Plan an elective caesarean section for her next birth

subtopic_detail: When contraception can be stopped in a woman using progestogen only pills at fifty three
stem:
A 53-year-old woman attends your general practice for a repeat prescription. She has taken a progestogen only pill continuously for nine years and has had no bleeding at all for the past four years.

She asks whether she still needs contraception, saying she is certain she has gone through the menopause and that her friend was told to have a blood test to prove it. She has no hot flushes and no vaginal dryness. She is a non smoker, her blood pressure is normal, and she has no personal or family history of venous thromboembolism or breast cancer.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 70 beats per minute, blood pressure 122/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 15 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Body mass index 26 kg/m2, no abnormality on abdominal or pelvic examination
data_table.Contraceptive history: Progestogen only pill for nine years, amenorrhoeic for four years, no missed pills
data_table.Other: Non smoker, no vasomotor symptoms, cervical screening up to date and negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate advice?

options.text: Continue the pill until she is 55 and then stop it
Stop the pill now given four years without any bleeding
Check two follicle stimulating hormone levels and then stop
Change to the combined oral contraceptive pill until age 55
Stop the pill and use condoms alone until she turns 55

subtopic_detail: Severe hot flushes in a woman taking tamoxifen after breast cancer
stem:
A 49-year-old woman attends your general practice with severe hot flushes occurring around fifteen times a day and waking her four or five times each night. She has been exhausted for months and has started declining work and social commitments.

She completed treatment for an oestrogen receptor positive breast cancer eighteen months ago and takes tamoxifen. Her periods stopped during chemotherapy. She has tried reducing caffeine and alcohol, layered clothing and a bedroom fan without benefit. She has no depression on assessment, no vaginal bleeding, and her mood is low only in proportion to the sleep deprivation. She is not taking any antidepressant and has no history of seizures.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 76 beats per minute, blood pressure 124/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 15 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Body mass index 25 kg/m2, no lymphadenopathy, surgical breast examination unremarkable, no abnormality on abdominal examination
data_table.Symptom burden: Approximately fifteen daytime flushes and four to five night time waking episodes daily
data_table.Oncology history: Oestrogen receptor positive breast cancer treated eighteen months ago, currently on tamoxifen
data_table.Measures already tried: Caffeine and alcohol reduction, clothing layering, bedroom cooling, without benefit

lead_in: What would you first recommend?

options.text: Start systemic oestrogen therapy at the lowest effective dose
Start venlafaxine rather than any hormonal preparation
Start paroxetine as the non hormonal agent with best evidence
Recommend a phytoestrogen preparation available over the counter
Continue lifestyle measures alone and review her again in six months

subtopic_detail: Duration of anticoagulation after a pulmonary embolism at thirty weeks
stem:
You are the obstetric medicine registrar reviewing a 33-year-old woman who was diagnosed with a segmental pulmonary embolism at 30 weeks and started on therapeutic enoxaparin. She is now 38 weeks and well, with no chest pain and no breathlessness.

She has no personal history of previous thrombosis, no known thrombophilia and no family history of clotting problems. She asks how long she will need the injections after the baby is born, and whether she can change to tablets so she can stop injecting herself. She intends to breastfeed. A birth plan is being made for induction at 39 weeks.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 88 beats per minute, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 17 breaths per minute, SpO2 98 percent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius, fetal heart rate 142 beats per minute
data_table.Examination: Chest clear, calves soft and non-tender, symphysis fundal height 38 cm
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count and renal function within normal limits, platelets 232 x10^9/L, no thrombophilia identified
data_table.Treatment: Therapeutic enoxaparin since 30 weeks, well tolerated

lead_in: What is the most appropriate advice about the duration of treatment?

options.text: Stop the anticoagulation once she has given birth safely
Change to a direct oral anticoagulant as soon as she delivers
Continue therapeutic anticoagulation for six weeks postpartum
Reduce to a prophylactic dose for six weeks after she delivers
Continue therapeutic anticoagulation indefinitely from now on

subtopic_detail: Hypoglycaemia with coagulopathy and a raised urate at thirty six weeks
stem:
A 31-year-old woman in her first pregnancy presents at 36 weeks with five days of nausea, vomiting and upper abdominal discomfort, and two days of feeling confused and unusually thirsty.

Her blood pressure has been normal at every antenatal visit including today, and her urine shows no protein. She is jaundiced. Her blood glucose is 2.4 mmol/L despite eating this morning and has required a dextrose infusion. Her international normalised ratio is prolonged with a low fibrinogen, and her platelet count is only mildly reduced. Her haemoglobin is stable with no fragments on the film and her lactate dehydrogenase is only modestly raised. Fetal monitoring shows a reactive trace with normal growth.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 108 beats per minute, blood pressure 118/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, SpO2 98 percent on room air, temperature 36.9 degrees Celsius, fetal heart rate 148 beats per minute
data_table.Examination: Jaundiced, mildly encephalopathic with asterixis, tender right upper quadrant, no peripheral oedema, no hyperreflexia or clonus
data_table.Investigations: Blood glucose 2.4 mmol/L (3.5-7.8), international normalised ratio 2.1 (0.8-1.2), fibrinogen 1.2 g/L (2.0-4.5 in pregnancy), platelets 118 x10^9/L (150-400), bilirubin 92 micromol/L (less than 20), alanine aminotransferase 380 U/L (less than 35), urate 0.52 mmol/L (0.15-0.35), creatinine 138 micromol/L (45-90), no red cell fragments on film

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Start magnesium sulfate and manage her expectantly
Start ursodeoxycholic acid and plan birth at 37 weeks
Start plasma exchange for a thrombotic microangiopathy
Stabilise her and expedite the birth on the same day
Arrange viral hepatitis serology before any decision

subtopic_detail: Failure of lactation and fatigue after a major obstetric haemorrhage
stem:
A 29-year-old woman attends your clinic ten weeks after a birth complicated by a 3 litre postpartum haemorrhage that required six units of red cells and a period of hypotension in theatre.

She has never produced more than a few drops of milk despite intensive lactation support and has now stopped trying. She is profoundly tired, feels cold all the time and has not had a period. She has lost 4 kg without trying and describes feeling lightheaded when she stands up quickly. She is not breastfeeding, is taking no medication and her mood, while flat, does not meet criteria for a depressive episode on your assessment.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 92 beats per minute, blood pressure 94/58 mmHg lying and 78/50 mmHg standing, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.2 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Pale, loss of axillary and pubic hair, no goitre, no hyperpigmentation, no breast engorgement
data_table.Investigations: Sodium 128 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 4.2 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), free thyroxine 7 pmol/L (10-25), thyroid stimulating hormone 0.8 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), 9 am cortisol 62 nmol/L (185-624), prolactin low, follicle stimulating hormone and luteinising hormone both low
data_table.Obstetric history: Postpartum haemorrhage of 3 litres with transfusion and intraoperative hypotension

lead_in: What is the most important immediate treatment?

options.text: Start thyroxine replacement and review her again in four weeks
Start fludrocortisone for the postural drop in blood pressure
Give hypertonic saline to correct her sodium concentration
Start an antidepressant and arrange perinatal mental health review
Start hydrocortisone replacement before any other hormone

subtopic_detail: Sudden collapse with coagulopathy moments after artificial rupture of membranes
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar in the birth suite of a tertiary hospital. A 34-year-old woman at 39 weeks is being augmented in labour and you have just performed an artificial rupture of membranes.

Within two minutes she says she feels strange and cannot breathe, becomes acutely agitated, then loses consciousness. She has no pulse. There is no external bleeding at this point and the uterus is well contracted. She has no known allergy, no cardiac history, and had received no new medication in the preceding hour other than the oxytocin infusion already running. The fetal heart rate falls to 60 beats per minute. Blood taken as access is established shows a fibrinogen of 0.8 g/L and a markedly prolonged international normalised ratio.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse absent, blood pressure unrecordable, respiratory effort absent, SpO2 unrecordable, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius, fetal heart rate 60 beats per minute
data_table.Examination: Unresponsive with no palpable central pulse, uterus well contracted, no external haemorrhage, no urticaria, no angioedema, no bronchospasm audible
data_table.Investigations: Fibrinogen 0.8 g/L (2.0-4.5 in pregnancy), international normalised ratio markedly prolonged, platelets falling
data_table.Timing: Collapse within two minutes of artificial rupture of membranes

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Begin resuscitation with left uterine displacement and prepare for birth
Give intramuscular adrenaline and treat as anaphylaxis to oxytocin
Give a fluid bolus and transfuse red cells for concealed haemorrhage
Give intravenous thrombolysis for a presumed pulmonary embolism
Stop the oxytocin infusion and reassess her over the next few minutes
